title: The Steering Budget: Examples beat Knobs

paper.title: The Steering Budget: Examples beat Knobs
paper.abstract:
Abstract Generative models are steered with knobs — prompts, guidance scales,
property tags. Turn one as hard as you like and, past a point, it stops
moving the property you care about. We find that ceiling is not a
shortcoming of the model but a budget , set by the training data
before the model is trained: a property’s movable range splits in two
— the part a knob can reach, and a second, significant part that only
examples — concrete instances of what you want more of — can reach.
That second part is usually much larger, but not always, and the same
budget says so in advance. Reaching that second part takes a different move: instead of turning a
knob, you show the model examples, composed from what it already learned
rather than added to its training. A cheap audit of the training data
measures the budget; we give a recipe for building the example set that
reaches all of it. This buys two things a knob can’t. Reach: it moves a property
across the whole budget, not just the part a knob reaches. Expressiveness: it steers toward targets you can only specify by
example — including ones you can’t put into words. We turn these into
a handful of falsifiable claims and verify them in two unrelated
domains, image and crystal-structure generation — marking where a knob
is enough, and where only examples will do.

sections.heading:
Introduction — Steering with knobs, and steering by
example
sections.text: Suppose you have a generative model and you want it to lean a certain way — images with the feel of nature photography, crystal structures with a wider band gap. You reach for the controls: a prompt, a guidance scale, a property tag. Push them to their limit and they still carry the output only so far — the property you are steering settles well short of where you wanted it, and leaning harder does nothing. There is a more powerful move, and it is not a better knob. It is a change in what you hand the model . Instead of working the controls, you show it: a set of examples, and the instruction “more like these.” The examples are drawn from what the model already learned — you are not adding to its training or retraining it, only choosing which of its own material it works from. We find that this is the more powerful and more expressive way to steer — and, more surprisingly, that the gap between the two is not incidental but budgeted : how far each can move a property is fixed, before the model is trained, by the data it learned from. That budget is the spine of the paper. Examples play two different roles in it. The training data sets how big each part of the budget is — settled before the model exists. The examples you show at steering time are how you reach the part a knob cannot. The rest of this section previews the split, names the two operations, shows why the part a knob misses is the part people most often want — and ends on the targets an expert can recognize but cannot put into words.

sections.heading: Telling and showing
sections.text: So far we have two handles: knobs and examples. To say precisely how far each reaches, we need names for the two acts , not just the two things you hold. Turning a knob is telling . Handing over examples — “more like these” — is showing . These two acts have a precise structural difference, and it is the crux of the paper. Telling is conjunctive. Every label specification is an intersection: object = dog AND brightness = high AND size = large narrows the output set on each conjunct. You can only cut away. There is no natural way to say or — to ask for big bright dogs or small dark cats — without enumerating the union explicitly, which requires knowing the union in advance. Showing is disjunctive. An exemplar set can hold big bright dogs and small dark cats and medium fluffy spaniels at once, and “more like these” finds what is interesting about the collection without anyone naming the union. The or lives in the diversity of the set. The AND/OR observation. Telling can only narrow — it intersects. Showing can union — the disjunction lives in the spread of the examples, and never has to be articulated. That contrast — telling narrows, showing unions — is why showing reaches what telling cannot. The rest of the paper makes it precise, shows exactly how far each posture reaches, and tests the prediction in two unrelated domains.

sections.heading:
A budget on what steering can
reach
sections.text: Behind the AND/OR difference is something you can measure. Telling is the familiar operation: decide what you want and lean on the controls — the guidance dial, a descriptive token, an adapter — nudging the distribution one request at a time. Showing is the other: hand over a set of examples and let them shape a whole batch, never saying what they have in common. Here is what separates them. A cheap label — the class of an image, the chemistry of a crystal — sorts a model’s outputs into groups; call each a bin . Any property you care about, like brightness or a crystal’s band gap, varies two ways: within bins (golden retrievers differ in brightness) and between bins (a beach averages brighter than a wine cellar). Those two pieces add up to all the variation there is — and telling , working inside the bin you asked for, reaches only the within-bin part, while showing , choosing which bins the batch is drawn from, reaches the between-bin part. Each piece is a budget — a ceiling on how far that operation can move the property — fixed by the training data before the model is built. Preliminaries makes this precise. One question this raises: if the budget is set by the data, doesn’t that write the model out of the story? No — a stronger model produces a denser, more novel set of outputs, but that is a richer set, not a wider spread of any one property; we make the distinction precise later. So the two reach genuinely different ground. Much of what people actually want — outputs that meet two conditions at once, real variety across a batch, a preference you cannot put into words — lives in the part telling cannot reach. That is the ground showing covers.

sections.heading:
Steering toward what you can’t
name
sections.text: Reach — moving a property further than a knob can — is the measurable payoff, and most of the paper is about it. There is a second payoff, and it matters most exactly where naming the target is hardest. A materials scientist scrolling a list of candidate structures stops on one: that one looks promising. Pressed for a reason, they hesitate — the judgment is fast and reliable, the justification slow and partial. A film editor who keeps one take in ten is in the same position: the cut hangs together, but the rule that chose those takes resists being written down. This is the ordinary condition of expertise, not an edge case; Polanyi’s phrase is we know more than we can tell. Every knob asks the expert to tell anyway — to name the target in the model’s vocabulary before it can be pursued. Showing does not. The specification lives in the examples themselves, so you can steer toward a taste you can demonstrate but not articulate: keep the ten candidates you would have kept, hand them over, and ask for more like them. And because showing composes by union — the examples may disagree, and “more like these” finds what they share without anyone naming it — it reaches tastes, trade-offs, and combinations no single named target captures. This expressiveness is what the budget’s between-bin part pays for; we return to it, and to its uses, in Application .

sections.heading:
Why this matters even if you never use
exemplars
sections.text: You might expect the telling / showing split to matter only when you have exemplars in hand. It reaches further than that: it sits underneath some of the most familiar frustrations in generative modeling. Here is why. Almost every way we train or tune a model — fitting it to data, optimizing it against a reward, nudging it toward preferences — works one output at a time , pushing each toward “better.” Tuning output by output can sharpen each one, but it cannot build variety — because variety is not a property of any single output. It is a property of the whole collection , and the collection is exactly the ground showing governs and telling never reaches. So the harder you tune for quality, the less variety comes back. Anyone who has fine-tuned a model and watched it turn repetitive has met this. The variety did not evaporate for no reason: output-by-output tuning can only narrow it, never produce it; the variety lives between bins, and only showing reaches it. The field already has names for the symptoms, usually treated one by one: a model collapsing onto a handful of outputs ( mode collapse ); a tuned model that answers well but has lost its range (the alignment tax ); a model that games its score by overproducing one safe thing ( reward hacking ); a model that can satisfy two requirements on their own but not together ( compositional generalization ). One cause sits under all four: each asks output-by-output tuning to deliver something it structurally cannot — variety, coverage, a joint, all properties of the collection rather than of any single output — and that tuning can only concentrate, never supply it. Reaching them takes a move across the collection, which is what showing names. Alongside each phenomenon’s familiar drivers, Theory makes that tie explicit. The lost variety, it turns out, is part of the budget itself — used up by tuning, and put back only by acting on the collection.

sections.heading:
Evidence across two
domains
sections.text: We do not just argue this; we test it, in two fields that share no model, data, or code — a diffusion model trained on ImageNet, where the bins and the steering are easy to see, and a generator of crystal structures, where an expert routinely flags a promising candidate without being able to say why. This section previews what we find; Evidence has the numbers. Examples are the more powerful control in general — and the budget says exactly when. On crystals, choosing which chemistries a batch is drawn from moves a target tens to hundreds of times more than the model’s own “high band gap” dial — and still several times more when we replace that dial with the strongest within-chemistry knob we can build. On images, choosing which classes moves the semantic targets a guidance dial can barely touch. The advantage is not universal, and the framework predicts when knobs are powerful enough. In the image domain, we show that knobs are sufficient to move brightness, and can be made to improve aesthetics too — but only by drifting across bins. Examples express what a knob cannot. Ask for a batch that holds two opposing kinds at once — clean vehicles and clean food, or crystals spanning a materials trade-off — and a knob gives you one kind, or a blurred average of the two; only composing examples puts genuine instances of both in the batch. And the budget is real, not just bookkeeping. The split into the two parts is exact by construction. Properties aligned with the model’s training goals carry through to the trained model; some do not — and we show you can predict which will. Most of the checks are cheap to verify. The budget itself is a variance calculation on training data — it runs on a laptop. Only the last step, confirming that a real model behaves the way the budget predicts, has to generate samples; even that fit on a single machine with a GPU in a few hours.

sections.heading:
What the paper
contributes
sections.text: The rest of the paper turns the tell/show idea into something you can compute, test, and use. The central claim is this: the steerable mean-shift of a labeled property splits into a telling part and a showing part, both computable from training data before the model exists — and this reveals which targets telling cannot reach. Five contributions follow, in the order they arrive: • The distinction itself, made precise — telling and showing as two operations, and the AND/OR observation that fixes what each can express. • A budget you can compute in advance — the exact accounting that splits a property’s variation into a within-bin part (what telling reaches) and a between-bin part (what showing reaches), with a ceiling on each, from training data alone. • A unifying lens on four familiar problems — mode collapse, the alignment tax, reward hacking, and the failure to compose requirements, read as a single mismatch: telling sent to do a showing job. • Evidence in two unrelated fields — images and crystals — that composing examples is, in general, the stronger lever: it moves a target several-fold further than the strongest knob we could build wherever the budget is mostly between-bin, and it is the only way to cover two opposed properties in one batch (which neither prompting nor composing conditions can do). The budget also calls the cases where examples are not the move — the low-level scalars (image brightness, aesthetic) whose range sits mostly inside the bins, where a strong knob wins; a goal that is merely a batch average, which a single well-chosen category already meets — and the one place nothing helps: a property the model reproduces too poorly for any recipe to reach. • A recipe — even when you can’t name the target. When telling falls short, we show how to choose which categories to draw from: if you can score the target, find the categories that rank high on it in the training data. If you can’t — a preference you can only point to — use a handful of samples you like to choose categories for you by picking the categories they fall into. What’s new, and what isn’t. Steering by example is not itself new — example- and reference-conditioned generation take similar approaches. What’s new here is the articulation of the budget: a quantitative account, read from the training data, of how far telling and showing can each reach. (Related Work places it among these.)

sections.heading: When a knob is enough
sections.text: Examples are the stronger lever, but not everywhere — and the same budget that says when they win says when they are not worth the trouble. There are two such cases, each with a cheap check: • The knob already reaches. When little of a property’s variation sits between bins — its between-bin share is small — and a knob drives it directly, a knob is enough. Check: measure that between-bin share from the data; if it is small, the knob has the room. (Image brightness is the one such case we found.) • The model doesn’t reproduce the property. The budget is read off the data, so it transfers only to properties the model makes faithfully; for one it does not, no recipe reaches it. Check: audit a sample of the model’s own outputs against the data. In short: measure the budget first, and let it tell you whether to reach for examples at all.

sections.heading: Roadmap
sections.text: Preliminaries sets up the shared language in two pages — the bins, the two operations, the two budgets — and sends you on. Theory derives the two bounds, shows how the choice of exemplars scales what showing can reach, states the four falsifiable claims, and closes by connecting them back to the phenomena above. Evidence tests the claims in both fields. Application turns it into a recipe: measure your budget, measure how far telling already gets you, and — if a gap remains — read its shape to choose how to close it.

sections.heading:
Preliminaries — the cheap key and the expensive
target
sections.text: The introduction named two moves — telling and showing — and a budget that splits between them. This section makes all three precise: the bins, the two moves, and the two budgets. Everything after is built from them. A generative model hands you a stream of outputs, and you want to steer it — more of some kinds, fewer of others. Some of what makes an output desirable is cheap to read: the class of an image, the elements in a crystal. What you usually care about is expensive: whether an image looks good takes a second trained model, or a person, to judge; a crystal’s band gap — the number that decides whether it is a useful semiconductor — takes a physics simulation that can run for hours. These two reads — the cheap one and the expensive one — are most of the notation in this section. • The cheap read is a label P P , from a function π \pi (the classifier, the formula-reader): P = π ⁡ ( D ) P=\pi(D) for an output D D . • The expensive property is L L , from a function ψ \psi (the aesthetic scorer, the band-gap simulation): L = ψ ⁡ ( D ) L=\psi(D) . The one idea to carry: P P is a key, not a measurement. It sorts outputs into groups: every golden-retriever picture into one, every table-salt crystal into another. Call each group a bin . The whole paper is about steering the expensive L L by choosing how we work with the cheap bins P P gives us.

sections.heading: Bins
sections.text: Run π \pi over a pile of outputs and it drops each into a bin — one bin per distinct label. For the image model there is a “golden retriever” bin, a “ladybug” bin, one per class. For the crystal model π \pi reads (elements, atom count), so there is a (Si, O; 6) bin, a (Mg, O; 2) bin, and so on. With B B distinct labels there are B B bins, and P b P_{b} is the label of bin b b . (A real request carries more than the key — a guidance scale, a style token — the knobs of the introduction. P P is the part this paper turns on, so we fold those into “the controls” and set them aside for now; they return below as telling .)

sections.heading: What the model produces
sections.text: What is the model trained to make? More of whatever it learned from — and it is random : ask it once and you get one output; ask again, same request, and you get a different one. A request doesn’t pin down an output, it pins down a spread of outputs. What that spread looks like is fixed by the data the model trained on. So name that data: 𝒥 \mathcal{J} is the distribution of your training set. Train on ImageNet and 𝒥 \mathcal{J} is ImageNet’s distribution; train on a different collection and 𝒥 \mathcal{J} is different. The framework is computed relative to the data you used: your budget for a property is set by your training set. We never need 𝒥 \mathcal{J} itself — a distribution over whole images, or whole crystals. We need only its shadow on ( P , L ) (P,L) : pass each output through the cheap label P P and the property L L , and keep a few numbers per bin. That shadow is all the machinery ever touches, and it is concrete — just statistics of your data.

sections.heading: The working picture
sections.text: Now take the expensive property L L — the band gap — and look at how it varies across the bins. It varies two ways: • within a bin, the (Si, O; 6) crystals do not all share one band gap; • between bins, the averages differ — silicon oxides sit near 1 eV, magnesium oxides up near 7 eV. So picture B B columns, one per bin, each a cloud of L L values — every cloud has some spread, and the columns sit at different heights. One output’s band gap is one dot in one column. Figure 1: Each bin is a column of L values: every column has some spread (the within-bin variation) and sits at a height (the bin’s average). Some bins are tight and high, others wide and low. (Schematic — illustrative numbers, not measured data.) Each column is a bin; the dots are the L L values in it. A column’s spread is the within-bin variation; its height is the average. This is the picture to keep for the whole paper. (The image model looks the same: each class is a column, brightness varies within a class, and some classes — beaches — average brighter than others — coal mines.)

sections.heading: The audit
sections.text: The working picture reduces to three numbers per bin, and producing them is one fixed procedure — an audit : take a set of outputs, sort each into its bin via P P — cheap, so you bin them all — then score the expensive L L on a handful of outputs from each bin (few, because ψ \psi is dear, but enough to pin down the bin’s average and spread), and record, per bin, • its share w b w_{b} — the fraction of outputs that land in it; • its height g b g_{b} — the average L L in it; • its spread v b v_{b} — how much L L varies inside it. Those three numbers per bin are the audit’s output — its shadow on ( P , L ) (P,L) — and the entire input to everything that follows. Because π \pi is cheap but ψ \psi dear, the shares w b w_{b} come out exact — you bin everything — while the heights and spreads are estimates from the scored handful: a few per bin are enough for the targets steering cares about, more when L L varies mostly within bins. Application gives the rule for choosing the count, and the correction for sampling so few. You can run the very same procedure on two different sets of outputs: your training data ( audit 𝒥 \mathcal{J} ) or a batch of the model’s own samples ( audit G \mathrm{G} ). From here on those two terms mean precisely this — the binning and the three numbers — and the rest of the paper uses them without re-explaining.

sections.heading: Two ways to steer
sections.text: Say you want brighter images. Here are the two moves the introduction named, now made precise — and the rest of the paper turns on the difference between them. • Telling ( per-prompt steering ). Work within one bin — say “golden retriever” — and lean on the controls: turn up the guidance dial, add the token “bright”, attach an adapter. You shift that bin’s outputs toward its brighter end. In the picture: you stay in one column and pull its dots toward an end. • Showing ( exemplar steering ). Instead of describing the target, you hand the model a batch of examples and ask for more like them. Sorted through the cheap label P P , that batch is a mix of bins — a recipe “70% beach scenes, 30% snow,” written μ P \mu_{P} . It is the mix, not the individual examples, that the move turns on, so from here we describe showing by its recipe μ P \mu_{P} over bins. In the picture: you choose which columns the batch comes from. You hand over examples, but what steers is the mix of bins they fall into — that is the one shift in vocabulary to keep. Telling works one column; showing weights different columns. They reach different parts of the picture. We make all of this precise next.

sections.heading: Two budgets
sections.text: The total spread of L L — its variance across the data — splits cleanly into the two parts the picture shows, and each move draws on one: Figure 2: The variance budget: the total spread of L splits into the within-column part (the within-bin budget, telling) and the between-column part (the between-bin budget, showing). ( Schematic — illustrative numbers, not measured data; the measured crystal split, e.g. band gap E / ( E + T ) = 0.98 E/(E{+}T)=0.98 , is in Evidence §4.) • Telling draws on the spread within a column — the within-bin budget T T . • Showing draws on the spread between columns — the between-bin budget E E . They sum to the whole spread, exactly: Var 𝒥 ​ ( L ) = ∑ b w b ​ v b ⏟ T ​ (within) + ∑ b w b ​ ( g b − g ¯ ) 2 ⏟ E ​ (between) , g ¯ = ∑ b w b ​ g b . \mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{J}}(L)\;=\;\underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{b}w_{b}\,v_{b}}_{T\ \text{(within)}}\;+\;\underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{b}w_{b}\,(g_{b}-\bar{g})^{2}}_{E\ \text{(between)}},\qquad\bar{g}=\textstyle\sum_{b}w_{b}\,g_{b}. A budget is a variance — the room available, nothing more. It says how far a property could be moved, not what any particular move does with it. The two moves each draw on one budget. Telling reweights within a bin, so it draws on T T ; showing reweights across bins with the recipe μ P \mu_{P} , so it draws on E E . Either way, the move shifts the average L L of what you generate, and that shift is at most χ 2 ⋅ budget \sqrt{\chi^{2}\cdot\text{budget}} — where χ 2 \chi^{2} measures how hard the move pushes from the original mix. The budgets are fixed by the three numbers, before the model is built . So the deciding difference between the moves is not how hard you push but which budget each can touch at all — T T for telling, E E for showing. Telling cannot cross bins. We have written the goal as the batch’s average L L , but it can be any property of the batch — its spread, or whether it covers two kinds at once. Theory derives the bounds, unpacks χ 2 \chi^{2} , and shows which move each kind of goal needs.

sections.heading: Data audit, model audit
sections.text: Everything so far has audited the training data 𝒥 \mathcal{J} — the budget is read off the data, before the model is even built. But what you ultimately care about is what the model produces: an audit of its own outputs, G \mathrm{G} . So why should the data audit tell you anything about the model’s? Because a generative model is trained to reproduce its data. For a property it reproduces well, the model’s outputs fall into the bins with the same shares, heights, and spreads as the data — the model audit matches the data audit — so the cheap data audit (no model, no sampling) stands in for it. The catch is that the model is not trained on your property L L . It is trained to reproduce the data as a whole — to predict the next token, to denoise toward real samples — and L L is just something you happen to care about. So the data audit stands in faithfully only when L L is something the model reproduces well. A crystal generator’s density — read straight off the shape it draws — comes out matching the data; its stability — an energy that a small error in the structure throws off — does not, and there the model audit drifts from the data’s. When you are not sure a property carries, don’t guess — check it: sample the model, audit those outputs, and compare them to the data’s bin by bin — the two numbers to read are the drift δ \delta (did the bin means move?) and the spread ratio ρ \rho (did the within-bin variety carry?). Application gives that check step by step, Evidence runs it across easy and hard properties in both domains, and Theory ’s Scope marks where the data audit holds and where it breaks. (A fine-tuned model reproduces a reshaped version of the data — Theory handles that too.) Every symbol above is also collected in a one-page table, grouped by kind, in the Appendix (§A0, Notation ) — for reference when a symbol turns up later without its introduction nearby.

sections.heading: Where to go from here
sections.text: You now have the working picture — B B bins of L L , the two moves, the two budgets. The rest of the paper builds on it in order: • Theory derives where the two square-root bounds come from, shows how the choice of recipe μ P \mu_{P} scales showing’s reach (the χ 2 \chi^{2} factor), and states the falsifiable claims that follow — then closes with a short note on what this implies for familiar training phenomena (mode collapse, the alignment tax, and the like). (It also notes why variance is the right currency — a methodological choice: cruder measures like max-minus-min are noisy.) • Evidence tests those claims in two unrelated domains. • Application turns the result into a recipe: how to measure your own budget, tell whether telling already suffices, and pick the construction that closes the gap if it does not. A reader who wants the practice before the derivations can jump straight to Application and refer back.

sections.heading:
Theory — How far telling and showing
reach
sections.text: Preliminaries set up the working picture and the two ways to steer. To recall: a generator G \mathrm{G} produces outputs D D ; a cheap key P = π ⁡ ( D ) P=\pi(D) sorts them into B B bins; the expensive target L = ψ ⁡ ( D ) L=\psi(D) fills each bin with a spread of values; and you steer L L two ways — telling stays inside one bin and nudges its outputs, while showing changes which bins the batch is drawn from. Preliminaries also named the two budgets — T T (within-bin) and E E (between-bin) — and their reaches. This section derives them. §1 shows how the total spread of L L splits into the two budgets. §2 derives how far each operation can move L L , how the recipe μ P \mu_{P} scales showing’s reach through a factor χ 2 \chi^{2} , and — given a goal — which operation it calls for and, when that is showing, the shape (curvature) of the recipe it needs. §3 states the falsifiable claims that follow, including how the data-side budget transfers to a real model. §4 then reads off what the budget implies for some familiar training phenomena, and §5 marks where the framework applies and where it stops. The detailed machinery, the case-by-case reach of each operation, and the full statement of the boundaries are in the Appendix . A practitioner can skip to Application . Recall the per-bin quantities: bin b b has share w b w_{b} , mean g b = 𝔼 𝒥 ​ [ L ∣ P b ] g_{b}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{J}}[L\mid P_{b}] , and within-bin variance v b = Var 𝒥 ​ [ L ∣ P b ] v_{b}=\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{J}}[L\mid P_{b}] .

sections.heading:
1. The budget: one variance, split in
two
sections.text: Take the property L L and ask where its variation across the data lives. Some sits within bins — outputs that share a key still differ in L L — and some sits between bins — different bins have different average L L . Those are the only two places it can live, and across the B B bins they add up exactly: Var 𝒥 ​ ( L ) ⏟ total = ∑ b w b ​ v b ⏟ T ​ (within-bin) + ∑ b w b ​ ( g b − g ¯ ) 2 ⏟ E ​ (between-bin) , g ¯ = ∑ b w b ​ g b . \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{J}}(L)}_{\text{total}}\;=\;\underbrace{\sum_{b}w_{b}\,v_{b}}_{T\ \text{(within-bin)}}\;+\;\underbrace{\sum_{b}w_{b}\,(g_{b}-\bar{g})^{2}}_{E\ \text{(between-bin)}},\qquad\bar{g}=\sum_{b}w_{b}\,g_{b}. T T is the within-bin spread averaged over bins — the room telling works in, since telling stays inside one bin. E E is the spread of the bin means — the room showing works in, since showing moves between bins. This identity is the law of total variance (Casella & Berger, 2002), exact for any ( π , L , 𝒥 ) (\pi,L,\mathcal{J}) — no overlap, no remainder. Its two terms are the room the two operations work in. The pieces here are elementary — the total-variance split and the Cauchy–Schwarz reweighting bound below are textbook; the contribution is not the mathematics but composing them into a cheap, pre-model, three-numbers-per-bin audit that forecasts the telling/showing crossover and, under a testable condition, carries to a trained model. And how the total divides is the practitioner’s to set through π \pi — finer bins move variance into E E , coarser into T T (at the extremes, one-output bins give T → 0 T\to 0 ; a single bin gives E → 0 E\to 0 ) — fixing, before any model exists, which operation has room to work. Note — the choice of variance. Why measure spread by variance rather than the range max ⁡ L − min ⁡ L \max L-\min L ? The range carries no within/between split, so it could not be divided into the two budgets at all; it is fixed by a single extreme output; and it is routinely exceeded by the model’s own outputs. Variance is the stable data-side quantity — a methodological choice, argued in full in the Appendix.

sections.heading: 2. The two reaches
sections.text: A budget is room ; the reach is how far an operation can actually move the average of L L , given that room. Both operations move it the same way — by reweighting : shifting how much of the batch comes from where. Reweighting obeys a single law — depart from a set’s own proportions and the most you can move its average is set by how far you departed: | Δ ​ 𝔼 ​ [ L ] | ≤ χ 2 ⋅ σ 2 , |\Delta\,\mathbb{E}[L]|\leq\sqrt{\chi^{2}\cdot\sigma^{2}}, where σ 2 \sigma^{2} is the variance of the set you reweight and the Pearson χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence measures the size of the departure — 0 0 when you change nothing, growing as you pile weight onto rare values. This is Cauchy–Schwarz (derived just below). One standard deviation, σ 2 \sqrt{\sigma^{2}} , is only the gentle case χ 2 = 1 \chi^{2}=1 ; push harder and you move further, at a price that grows as χ 2 \sqrt{\chi^{2}} . The two operations differ in which set they are allowed to reweight. Telling stays inside the bin you named. A prompt or a guidance knob can shift weight among the outputs within a bin, but it cannot move an output into a different bin — it cannot change which class, or which chemistry, the sample is. So telling reweights within bins, and the variance it acts on is the within-bin budget T T : | Δ ​ 𝔼 ​ [ L ] | ≤ χ tell 2 ⋅ T . |\Delta\,\mathbb{E}[L]|\leq\sqrt{\chi^{2}_{\text{tell}}\cdot T}. Pushing the controls harder raises χ tell 2 \chi^{2}_{\text{tell}} , but telling is still confined to the room a bin already has. In practice the controls push gently : turning the guidance dial to its limit moves a bin’s average only a little, so χ tell 2 \chi^{2}_{\text{tell}} stays small and telling’s realized reach sits near the unit-effort scale T \sqrt{T} (Evidence measures it). Showing changes the bin mix instead. Its design knob is the recipe μ P \mu_{P} , a distribution over the bins (Preliminaries: “70% beaches, 30% snow”). Draw bins in the data’s own proportions — μ P = 𝒥 P \mu_{P}=\mathcal{J}_{P} — and you reproduce the data, shifting nothing; to move the average you must depart from 𝒥 P \mathcal{J}_{P} , drawing more from the high- L L bins and fewer from the low. The shift you get is Δ ​ 𝔼 ​ [ L ] = ∑ b ( μ P ​ ( b ) − 𝒥 P ​ ( b ) ) ​ g b , \Delta\,\mathbb{E}[L]=\sum_{b}\big(\mu_{P}(b)-\mathcal{J}_{P}(b)\big)\,g_{b}, a sum across bins of how much you over- or under-weight each bin times that bin’s average — an inner product of two lists. And an inner product is at most the product of the two magnitudes ( Cauchy–Schwarz ): one is how far μ P \mu_{P} departs from 𝒥 P \mathcal{J}_{P} , the Pearson χ 2 \chi^{2} -divergence χ 2 ( μ P ∥ 𝒥 P ) = ∑ b ( μ P ​ ( b ) − 𝒥 P ​ ( b ) ) 2 𝒥 P ​ ( b ) , \chi^{2}(\mu_{P}\|\mathcal{J}_{P})=\sum_{b}\frac{(\mu_{P}(b)-\mathcal{J}_{P}(b))^{2}}{\mathcal{J}_{P}(b)}, the other the spread of the bin means, E \sqrt{E} . So showing reweights across bins and reaches the between-bin budget E E : | Δ ​ 𝔼 ​ [ L ] | ≤ χ 2 ( μ P ∥ 𝒥 P ) ⋅ E , |\Delta\,\mathbb{E}[L]|\leq\sqrt{\chi^{2}(\mu_{P}\|\mathcal{J}_{P})\cdot E}, largest when the recipe piles its extra weight on the bins with the most extreme means. The χ 2 \chi^{2} depends only on ( μ P , 𝒥 P ) (\mu_{P},\mathcal{J}_{P}) — never on the label. The two reaches have the same form — χ 2 ⋅ budget \sqrt{\chi^{2}\cdot\text{budget}} — so the asymmetry between telling and showing lives in two other places. First, and decisively, it is structural : telling is locked to the within-bin budget T T and showing to the between-bin budget E E , a division fixed by the key π \pi before any model exists. Telling cannot reach E E at all , because it cannot change bin membership — that is the heart of the matter, and it holds no matter how hard the controls are pushed. Second, it is empirical : pushed to its limit a knob departs only slightly from its bin’s own proportions ( χ 2 \chi^{2} near 1 1 ), while a recipe departs sharply from the data’s mix ( χ 2 \chi^{2} of order 100 100 ) — so showing realizes a far larger χ 2 \chi^{2} , and moves the mean far more (Evidence measures both). These two halves are easy to conflate, so we separate them. The structural half is true by definition : we call an operation telling precisely when it holds the key π \pi fixed — reweighting within a bin without changing bin membership — so “telling only reaches T T ” by definition. (Note: In one experiment in Evidence, we see that a knob pushed hard enough to rival showing turns out to leave its bin. Since it no longer is confined to a bin, we call that showing). The empirical content is the separate, non-definitional part: that real, deployed knobs realize only χ 2 ≈ 1 \chi^{2}\approx 1 , two orders below a recipe’s χ 2 ≈ 100 \chi^{2}\approx 100 — and that the one knob strong enough to close the gap does so only by ceasing to hold π \pi fixed, i.e. by becoming showing. Both reaches are ceilings — computable from the bins before any model is built, and bounding the most an operation could move the mean, not predicting what it will. They come from Cauchy–Schwarz, tight only when all the weight sits on the most extreme members; a real recipe lands below, and the gap widens as χ 2 \chi^{2} grows (Claim 2). Whether a model even delivers the in-support reach is Claim 1.

sections.heading:
Which operation a goal
needs
sections.text: The reaches give the room ; which operation claims it is the reach question . A shift small enough to find inside your bin — under T \sqrt{T} — needs only telling : lean on the knobs. A larger one is out of any single bin’s within-reach, so you must show — act on the mix of bins μ P \mu_{P} . Telling steers within the bin you are in; it never chooses the bin. Some goals you cannot even write down — a quality you only recognize by eye; there you show directly, letting a set of examples’ own mix of bins be the recipe (the lift ; Application). For a goal you can write, one question remains once you are showing: the shape of the recipe.

sections.heading:
Curvature — the shape of the showing
recipe
sections.text: The reach question decided whether to show; curvature decides how . Run a recipe μ \mu over the bins and you get a batch of outputs; the goal is some number you read off that batch — its average band gap, say, or whether it holds both a wide-gap and a stable structure. So the goal is a function F ⁡ ( μ ) F(\mu) of the recipe, maximized over the simplex Δ = { μ ≥ 0 , ∑ b μ ( b ) = 1 } \Delta=\{\mu\geq 0,\ \sum_{b}\mu(b)=1\} . Its curvature places the maximum: • F F convex (linear included) → a vertex of Δ \Delta : concentrate μ \mu on one bin. Say you want the batch’s average band gap as high as possible: F ⁡ ( μ ) = ∑ b μ ⁡ ( b ) ​ g b F(\mu)=\sum_{b}\mu(b)\,g_{b} is linear in μ \mu , so it is largest with all the weight on the single highest-gap chemistry. A rate — the fraction of the batch past a bar — behaves the same way. That one bin is what the audit finds, so concentrating on it is still showing (reach E E ), not telling. • F F strictly concave → the interior: spread μ \mu across bins. Now you want a batch that covers two kinds at once — a wide-gap structure and a stable one. No single chemistry is both; each sits in one corner, so a mix of a wide-gap bin and a stable bin holds both, and the blend beats any lone bin. Diversity behaves the same way. Both are showing ; naming the goal (telling) reaches neither. So the split — E E against T T — sets how far steering can move the mean; curvature sets whether the showing recipe concentrates on one bin or spreads across many. More than one property. Take two properties A A and B B , and mark each bin as a point on a plane — its mean of A A across, its mean of B B up. A recipe’s batch lands at the blend of those points, so its reachable averages fill the convex hull of the bins. The goal is usually to span the Pareto front — the trade-off edge of non-dominated points — which is a coverage goal, so it needs a mixture of specialist bins (showing): a single bin is just one point on the edge. The one escape is within-bin spread — a single bin’s draws fan out into an ellipsoid, and if that reaches the front’s corners it can cover the edge alone; but the wider the front, and the more properties you stack, the less one ellipsoid reaches, so specialist bins (showing) become the only way. (The crossover, and how it tightens with the number of properties, is in the Appendix.) Figure 3: Two properties. Each bin is a point in the (mean- A A , mean- B B ) plane; a recipe’s batch average is a blend of those points, so its reachable averages fill the convex hull (shaded). Spanning the Pareto front — the non-dominated upper-right edge — takes a mixture of specialist bins (showing); a single bin is one point, and its within-bin spread (the ellipse) reaches the corners only when the front is narrow. (Schematic — illustrative, not measured data.)

sections.heading:
3. What follows: four falsifiable
claims
sections.text: The framework is not vacuous; a few sharp, falsifiable claims fall out, and Evidence tests each across two unrelated domains. 1. The split is exact, and it carries to the model. T + E = Var 𝒥 ​ ( L ) T+E=\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{J}}(L) to machine precision for any ( L , π , 𝒥 ) (L,\pi,\mathcal{J}) , and the split moves with π \pi as described in §1. It is not only a fact about the data: for a target the model reproduces well, the model’s own outputs carry the same split, so the data-side budget describes the model too. But the model is never trained on your target L L — only to reproduce the data as a whole — so a target carries faithfully only insofar as the model reproduces it , and that varies: geometry rides the training objective closely, a sharp energy loosely. Auditing a model therefore means asking how well it reproduces the particular target you chose . This is the framework’s one empirical input, which Evidence tests across easy-to-hard targets, with the diagnostics — drift δ \delta , spread ratio ρ \rho — read per target. 2. The two reaches touch orthogonal budgets — telling is confined to the within-bin budget T T , showing reaches the between-bin budget E E ; each bounded by χ 2 ⋅ budget \sqrt{\chi^{2}\cdot\text{budget}} and computable before a model exists. 3. A goal’s curvature sets the shape of the showing recipe (§2). Convex/linear goals — batch averages, rates, conjunctions — peak at one bin, so showing concentrates μ P \mu_{P} there (the bin the audit finds); concave goals — coverage, diversity — peak at a blend, so showing spreads μ P \mu_{P} across bins, and no single bin reaches them. Both are showing; naming the goal (telling) reaches neither. For several properties at once the reachable averages are the convex hull of the bins, and covering a trade-off frontier is such a spread goal. (The Intro’s AND/OR observation, made quantitative.) 4. Training reshapes the budget — predictably. Plain likelihood training aims only to reproduce the data — exact for the crystal LM, a variational bound for the diffusion image model — and its objective is minimized when the model’s conditional is the data’s, so at the optimum the budget is the data’s, unchanged. Fine-tuning deliberately departs from that: filtering or RLHF reweights 𝒥 \mathcal{J} into a reshaped 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} , and the new per-bin numbers are computable from the old ones and the recipe — so recompute the budget from 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} and you predict the tuned model’s reaches without ever sampling it. One boundary: a fine-tune can pull so far from 𝒥 \mathcal{J} that nothing data-side is left to recompute from — there, audit the model’s own outputs instead. (The machinery and the reshaped 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} : Appendix .)

sections.heading:
4. One mechanism, four
phenomena
sections.text: The budget also explains a familiar frustration: the harder we tune a model to score well, the more variety it loses — and the same mechanism appears to run under several named problems at once. Take an image generator and fine-tune it for looks — the standard RLHF/DPO move. Underneath, the move is precise: it multiplies each output’s share of the distribution by a factor set by that output’s score, 𝒥 ′ ​ ( D ) ∝ 𝒥 ⁡ ( D ) ​ e R ⁡ ( D ) / β , \mathcal{J}^{\prime}(D)\;\propto\;\mathcal{J}(D)\,e^{R(D)/\beta}, where R ⁡ ( D ) R(D) is the score an output earns — here, its aesthetics — and β \beta is how hard you push (smaller β \beta , harder push). Outputs that score well get scaled up; the rest get scaled down. (This is the same reshaped 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} that Claim 4 routes fine-tunes through.) Watch what that does to our columns of bins. Within “golden retriever,” the best-looking retriever swells and the rest fade — the column narrows. Across classes, the photogenic ones (lakes, sunsets) grow while the drab ones (parking lots) shrink — the lineup of columns narrows too. Push harder ( β → 0 \beta\to 0 ) and it ends in one place: a single image, the highest-scoring one, everything else gone. Both kinds of spread have collapsed to nothing — the within-bin T T and the between-bin E E . And here is the crux. A reward scores one output at a time , and variety is not a property of any one output — it lives in the collection . So a per-output objective has nothing in it that can even see spread; it can only concentrate. To produce that spread you must act on the collection itself — choose the mix of bins. That is exactly what showing does: its recipe μ P \mu_{P} is the only lever on the between-bin budget E E from §2 — the part a per-output objective can never reach. Tuning collapses that spread; only showing realizes it. One exception proves the rule. Objectives that score a whole set — contrastive losses, batch-diversity penalties — genuinely can reward spread. But standard RLHF and DPO do not; and even a contrastive batch is a shuffled random sample pushed apart, not a designed mix of bins — it sees a batch without choosing the collection, which is what showing does. So one trade sits under four familiar problems — each buys per-output quality by collapsing collection spread a per-output method cannot recover: • Mode collapse — collection spread driven to the floor; the model parrots a handful of outputs. • The alignment tax — the diversity a tuned model loses is the spread it traded away for polish. • Reward hacking — hand it a reward to chase and it sprints to the single highest-scoring output. • Compositional generalization — asking for two things at once ( A and B ) needs outputs that already have both, and concentration only narrows. Showing can find the joint by drawing from the bins that hold it; per-output tuning never reaches it. Read this way, the four are one mechanism wearing four names: collection-level spread that per-output training collapses and only showing restores. Each still has its own familiar driver — the architecture, the data, a badly-chosen reward — and those hold; what the framework adds is a common cause beneath all four — the between-bin spread they narrow and cannot recover, which only showing reaches; an interpretation the framework invites.

sections.heading:
5. Scope — where this
applies
sections.text: We want to be precise about where the framework applies and where it does not. It applies to the mean shift of a labeled property, achieved by selection, in a model that matches its data ( 𝒥 \mathcal{J} , or the reshaped 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} after a standard fine-tune). There are degenerate extremes where it does not. The bound is a forecast : a real model can fall short of it (contraction) or, off the data’s support, exceed it (expansion). And it bounds the size of a mean shift — not the literal extremes of a property, and not the value of a set-level goal like coverage or diversity. For those goals the framework still says which operation reaches them — a mixture, showing (§2) — just not how large the metric gets. The full list of edges — off-support ( χ 2 → ∞ \chi^{2}\to\infty ), heavy-tailed bin means, the steered-batch variance, multi-property targets, leaving the selection regime — sits in the Appendix , each with a cheap check.

sections.heading: Pointer
sections.text: For practical use: Application . For empirical verification of the claims: Evidence . For the shared setup and notation: Preliminaries . For the detailed machinery (data-to-model bridge), the case-by-case reach of each operation, and the full boundary statement: the Appendix .

sections.heading:
Evidence — The same claims, in two unrelated
domains
sections.text: Theory made its predictions on paper. This section asks whether real generative models, on real data, obey them. The theory hands us a budget : for any target, the total variation splits into a piece that telling can reach and a piece that only showing can. What we don’t yet know is whether any of it survives a real model — whether the split leaks, whether a model reaches past its budget, whether fine-tuning breaks the accounting. To keep any one result from being a quirk of a single setup, we test in two domains that share no model, no data, no labels, and no scoring code. A prediction that holds in both is hard to explain away; it reads as a property of the framework. Vocabulary from Preliminaries : a cheap key sorts each output into a bin ; the within-bin budget T T is what telling reaches, the between-bin budget E E what showing reaches.

sections.heading: The two test beds
sections.text: Images — the legible track. A pretrained DiT-XL/2-256 (a diffusion model that turns a class label into an image), used as-is. The key is the class a frozen ResNet-50 reads off each image, so each of ImageNet’s 1000 classes is a bin. We steer seven plain measurements: brightness , a learned aesthetic score, compressed file size per megapixel (a stand-in for visual busyness), and four CLIP content scores — how well an image matches “a photo of an animal / a vehicle / food / nature.” You can inspect any bin’s images directly. Crystals — the consequence track. A pretrained encoder–decoder that generates a crystal structure to meet requested properties, trained on data derived from Alexandria, a large database of computed materials. The key is chemistry — the element set and atom count, read off the output. We steer band gap, energy above hull (distance from the stability frontier; zero is stable), density, dielectric constant, and one collection-level score — Combined , the fraction of generated structures that are at once novel, unique, and at least metastable. Cost. The image study runs in a few hours on a single GPU. The data-side claims (Claim 1, the Claim 2 bounds) are cheaper still: they need only the audit’s shadow — per-bin share, mean, and variance, 132 KB in all — and reproduce with numpy alone, no model and no ImageNet. The companion repo ships it; verify_dataside.py checks them in under a second.

sections.heading:
What we set out to
establish
sections.text: Four claims, each tested in both domains: # Claim 1 The budget splits exactly, the split moves as you change the bins, and it carries to the model 2 Telling and showing reach different parts of the budget — and we measure how much further showing reaches than a knob (bins vs knobs) 3 An average over a batch is reached by concentrating on one bin; a spread goal only by a mix of bins — both are showing, while naming (telling) reaches neither 4 Training changes the budget, but in a way you can predict The rest takes them one at a time, images first. The headline — how much further showing reaches than the best knob, and the between-bin share that says when — lives inside Claim 2, where we pit bins against the strongest knob each domain allows, property by property.

sections.heading:
Claim 1 — The budget splits exactly, moves with the bins,
and carries to the
model
sections.text: Three checks: the split is real, it moves with the bins, and it survives the model.

sections.heading: 1. The split is exact
sections.text: Total spread = spread inside the bins + spread between them, exactly. Images , brightness, bins the 1000 classes. Total variance 0.0181; within-class (one photo in sun, another in shade) averages 0.0151; between-class (snowfields brighter than coal) 0.0030. They sum to 0.0181. Crystals , energy-above-hull, bins the chemistry. Over 225,000 structures the total is 584 (meV/atom); within-chemistry spread is 22, between chemistries 562. They sum to 584. This is the law of total variance , an identity — so the exact match is not evidence for anything; it just confirms we measured the three numbers right. Claim 1’s empirical weight is in the next two parts — does the split move as predicted, and does it survive the model — and in Claims 2–4.

sections.heading:
2. Coarser bins shift the
split
sections.text: Make the bins coarser and variation moves from between to inside, as predicted. Images : merge the 1000 classes at random into 50 — within rises 0.0151 → 0.0179, between falls 0.0030 → 0.0002, total unchanged. Crystals : drop the atom count, keep only the element set — within 22 → 120, between 562 → 464, total unchanged. Figure 4: Claim 1: the brightness budget, fine bins versus coarse — the split is exact in both, and coarsening shifts it toward within-bin. That the split moves with the bins raises a fair worry: is the budget then just an artifact of an arbitrary key? No — it tracks meaningful structure, not the bin count. Recomputing the image split under several keys, the between-bin share’s ordering across targets is stable from 1000 classes down to a structured 50-bin grouping (class-aligned targets stay high, pixel-level targets stay low); only a random 50-bin key collapses the between-bin share to near zero for every target. A structured and a random key of the same 50-bin size differ roughly eighteen-fold — so what the budget reads is the key’s structure, not its resolution. (Same on crystals: the carry-over ordering below holds across element-set and atom-count keys.)

sections.heading:
3. Does the split carry through the
model?
sections.text: The split is a fact about the data; it matters only if the model reproduces it. A model can miss two ways: a bin lands in the wrong place (its average is off — the drift δ), or it holds the wrong amount of spread inside (the spread ratio ρ). We checked both. Do the bin averages land where the data says? Only when the property is close to what the model was trained to produce. The model isn’t trained on these properties — the crystal model learns to get a structure’s tokens right, DiT to get pixels right — so a property comes out right only if getting the tokens (or pixels) right forces it to. Per-bin agreement (correlation between the model’s per-chemistry averages and the data’s), with 95% confidence intervals from bootstrapping over chemistries and three generation seeds: • density 0.985 [0.91, 1.00] — fixed by the structure’s shape, which the tokens fix, so it carries tightly; • bonding plausibility 0.879 [0.04, 0.97] — the intermediate rung, and its wide interval says so: the point estimate lands between density and stability as predicted, but few ionic chemistries enter its fit, so bonding alone is pinned down only loosely; • stability 0.488 [0.17, 0.71] — a few stray atoms flip a structure off the frontier, so the tokens pin it down only loosely; its agreement is both lower and far less certain. Figure 5: Claim 1: how well the model’s per-chemistry averages match the data’s — 0.99 for density, 0.88 for bonding, 0.49 for stability, with 95% CIs (1 is exact, 0 is none). And we did not only measure this ordering — we predicted it before running the audit. From a small independent pilot, using only cheap pre-measurement signals (how often the model’s outputs even land in the data’s bins, plus the early drift δ and spread ratio ρ), we committed in advance — timestamped in the repo — to the ordering density > bonding > stability, density above ~0.9 and stability below ~0.4. The converged audit confirmed the ordering exactly (0.99 / 0.88 / 0.49); the magnitude calls were close, stability landing at 0.49 — a touch above its ~0.4 band, the one number that overshot. The ordering rests on the point estimates, which are cleanly ranked; the two ends — density high, stability low — are firm, while the middle rung (bonding) carries a wide interval and is the least certain of the three. So carry-over is a prediction the data makes ahead of time , not a pattern read off afterward — which is exactly what lets you trust the budget on a property before you have measured it on the model. So where the agreement is high and tight — density, and brightness on images — the budget you read off the data is the one the model produces; steer by it. Where it is low and uncertain — stability — the data audit is an unreliable guide, so measure the model directly instead. And stability’s low score is the property genuinely failing to carry, not a noisy yardstick: re-scoring it with a cleaner ensemble label leaves the agreement essentially unchanged (0.42 vs 0.49), and restricting to the chemistries whose labels are most reliable does not raise it. Does each bin hold the right variety? This is the room telling works in. On images the model produces 0.96–1.14× the data’s within-bin spread (spread ratio ρ ≈ 1), across every target — so telling ’s part of the budget is real on the model, not just on paper. And the bin averages track too: for class-aligned targets — nature, animal, food — the model’s per-class means correlate with the data’s at r² 0.85–0.94 (the higher-spread brightness and aesthetic targets sit lower, 0.48–0.59, and need more samples to pin down). The two checks are independent: one crystal model hit the right chemistries but filled them with unstable structures (high stability drift). Check both before trusting the budget on a new model.

sections.heading:
Claim 2 — Telling and showing reach different parts of the
budget
sections.text: Telling reweights within a bin; showing reweights across them. Two things follow — one structural, one we measured. Images. The experiment: take one target — the animal score — and try to move its batch average two ways, generating a batch each way and measuring how far the average moved from the model’s default. To tell , fix a class and turn classifier-free guidance up as hard as it goes (staying inside that one bin). To show , draw the batch from the classes whose animal-averages are highest. The figure plots how far each got: Figure 6: Claim 2: how far telling and showing can move a target’s average from where it starts — telling within one bin’s width, showing across the whole span between bins. Structurally , telling cannot leave the bin it is in, so it can only reach the within-bin budget T T ; showing moves mass across bins, so it reaches the between-bin budget E E . Same model, same target — different budget. And the effort each spends differs by two orders of magnitude. We measured the χ² each operation actually puts in: telling pushed to its limit (classifier-free guidance swept up to CFG = 15) moves the within-bin distribution by a χ² of only about 1 to 1.6 , while the exemplar recipes below reach χ² of order 100 . At every guidance scale the realized shift stayed under telling’s own within-bin ceiling √(χ²·T) — the exact counterpart of showing’s √(χ²·E) — so √T is not a wall telling hits, just the χ² ≈ 1 scale it can afford. In one line: both obey the same √(χ²·budget) law; telling is confined to the small budget T and can spend only χ² ≈ 1, showing reaches the large budget E and spends χ² ≈ 100 — and that is the whole of the asymmetry. Showing’s reach also grows the harder you concentrate the recipe. Drawing from the top 400, then 100, 25, and 8 of the 1000 classes, the realized shift climbed — animal score 0.031 → 0.051 (95% CI [0.029, 0.034] to [0.049, 0.053]), brightness 0.036 → 0.118 ([0.014, 0.059] to [0.085, 0.151]) — and every recipe stayed under the budget’s ceiling, √(χ²·E), with χ² measuring how far the recipe departs from the data’s own mix of bins. The ceiling rises faster than the reach, so here it is a true but loose cap: the top bins, weighted bluntly, don’t sit far enough apart to use all the room. Figure 7: Claim 2: as the recipe concentrates (χ² rising), showing’s realized shift grows and stays under the budget’s ceiling √(χ²·E). The ceiling climbs faster, so the cap is loose at high concentration; for brightness the model also falls short of the shift the budget allows. But the ceiling is loose only because the blunt top- k recipe spends its χ² inefficiently. There is a recipe that spends it optimally — the min-χ² direction, which puts exactly the bin weights the Cauchy–Schwarz bound is tight for — and there the ceiling stops being a cap and becomes a forecast . Steering one target with that recipe at a small shift, the realized move (0.0162) landed on the predicted ceiling (0.0195), inside the bootstrap CI [0.0114, 0.0209], while the blunt top- k recipe at the same χ² reached only a fraction of its ceiling. So the bound has two faces: a loose cap when you concentrate crudely, a tight prediction when you steer efficiently. (At larger shifts the min-χ² weights hit the non-negativity floor and the realized move falls back below the ceiling; the tight regime is the small-shift, in-simplex one.) Figure 8: Claim 2: the min-χ² recipe turns the ceiling into a forecast — at a small target shift the realized move meets the predicted ceiling √(χ²·E) (its CI includes the bound), and falls below only once the recipe saturates against the non-negativity floor. Crystals. Telling means pushing within one chemistry — there are knobs (the property-tag conditioning the model was trained with, e.g. a “high band gap” or “stable” tag, turned up like a guidance scale), but once the chemistry is fixed they barely move the result: the chemistry has already set most of what you get, and the tags only nudge within it. Showing means choosing which chemistries to draw from, and it dials the Combined score smoothly from 0.2 to 0.8 — the gap between the two reaches, as wide as the framework predicts.

sections.heading:
How much further: bins versus knobs, and where the
crossover
falls
sections.text: Start with the fair, knob-proof number. At matched effort telling can spend what it has only inside the bins and reaches at most χ 2 ​ T \sqrt{\chi^{2}\,T} ; showing spends the same effort across bins and reaches χ 2 ​ E \sqrt{\chi^{2}\,E} . The common effort cancels, so their ratio is E / T \sqrt{E/T} — fixed by the data before any knob exists, and something no knob can argue its way out of. For the three crystal targets it is 6.8 (band gap), 3.2 (density) and 1.1 (stability): effort for effort, showing reaches several times further, and most where the budget is most between-bin. That is the ceiling. What a real knob realizes is a separate question — and it is the one a skeptic presses: maybe the knobs we tried were weak. So we pushed the knob as hard as each domain allows. Crystals. The deployed property tag is a weak knob: fix the chemistry and it realizes almost no effort ( χ 2 ≈ 1 \chi^{2}\approx 1 ), so the realized gap is even wider than the structural ceiling — target E / ( E + T ) E/(E{+}T) knob shift bin shift realized bin / knob band gap 0.98 0.003 2.71 ≈800× density 0.96 0.09 8.40 ≈91× stability (metastable rate) 0.57 0.009 0.385 ≈41× — every knob’s 95% CI through zero, every bin’s clear of it. (Because the knob moves essentially nothing, its CI straddling zero, the realized ratio has a near-zero denominator and is unstable — read it as “the tag does nothing,” and trust the knob-free E / T \sqrt{E/T} column above as the equal-effort number.) But a tag is not the strongest knob a chemistry allows. The strongest is best-of-twelve : generate a dozen candidates in a fixed chemistry and keep the best by the property scorer — the largest reweighting a per-output selector can do, at matched effort χ 2 ≈ 5.3 \chi^{2}\approx 5.3 . Even this loses, by 26× / 14× / 4.8× on gap / density / stability. On crystals the sweep holds from the weak tag all the way up to the strongest knob that stays inside a bin. Images. Here the strongest knob is more powerful, and it changes the story — in the framework’s favour. We built a learned soft-prompt : a continuous conditioning vector warm-started at the best class and optimised directly against the target scorer, the strongest single-conditioning knob we can imagine. Against it the contest turns clean — the bin/knob ratio now rises monotonically : target E / ( E + T ) E/(E{+}T) E / T \sqrt{E/T} (equal-effort) bin / strongest knob (realized) brightness 0.17 0.45 0.29 aesthetic score 0.27 0.61 0.41 vehicle content 0.57 1.15 3.0 animal content 0.72 1.60 2.9 With a strong enough knob, two targets flip : on brightness and aesthetic — the two lowest- E / ( E + T ) E/(E{+}T) scalars — the learned knob beats bins, while on the two high-share semantic targets it still loses by about three. But it wins only by leaving its bin : on those two targets the winning images land almost entirely outside the class they started from. So the experiment lets us construct a case where a knob wins, but only by breaking the bin barrier that defines telling in the first place. One caveat keeps this honest. DiT’s guidance conditions on the ImageNet class — which is our key π \pi — so on images “telling stays inside its bin” is close to true by construction, and the image contest is best read as illustration. The crystal knob is the cleaner test: the property tag (band-gap, stability) is a different handle from the chemistry key, so a tag that moves nothing while chemistry selection moves the property is genuine evidence, not a tautology of the setup. The two domains together — one where the knob and key coincide, one where they are distinct — bound the claim from both sides. That is the whole result, stated cleanly. It is not that examples always beat knobs. E / T \sqrt{E/T} is the fair comparison; best-of-twelve shows no within-bin knob escapes it; the soft-prompt shows the only escape is to stop being a knob — and the budget tells you, in advance, the one regime (low E / ( E + T ) E/(E{+}T) ) where that escape is worth making. The between-bin share is a number you read off the data before generating anything, and it names its own exceptions: brightness and aesthetic, its two lowest values.

sections.heading: Choosing the key
sections.text: The whole budget is defined against a key π \pi — the partition into bins — so a fair question is how to pick one without knowing the answer first. The same between-bin share answers it. Enumerate a few cheap candidate keys (a classifier’s classes, k-means over a cheap feature, element-set for crystals), and for each score E / ( E + T ) E/(E{+}T) from the data alone — no generation. The key with the largest share is the one to use, and the score predicts the payoff: across candidate keys and targets, the data-side E / ( E + T ) E/(E{+}T) tracks the realised bin/knob ratio (rank correlation 0.88 on images; on crystals a key-quality that also credits carry-over recovers the operative element-set key), with a structureless random partition sitting at the floor. And if no candidate key has a large share, that is itself the answer: the target is intrinsically knob-shaped — which is exactly why aesthetic and brightness, whose variance no key concentrates between bins, are the two a strong knob wins. (This needs some cheap label to bin by; discovering a key with no labels at all we leave open.)

sections.heading:
Claim 3 — The goal’s kind sets the recipe: one bin for an
average, a mix for a
spread
sections.text: A goal is a property of the batch you generate, and the theory splits goals in two — and with them the shape of the showing recipe. Some are an average over the batch — a high average score, a high fraction clearing a bar — and the best recipe concentrates on the single best bin (which the audit must find; it is not the average bin). Others are about the batch’s spread — the batch must cover two different kinds of output at once — and no single bin can do that, so the recipe spreads across bins. Both are showing; naming the goal (telling) reaches neither. We test both kinds, in both domains, and each needs the recipe shape the theory predicts.

sections.heading:
An averaging goal: one bin
wins
sections.text: Start with a goal that looks like it needs a spread of bins but doesn’t. Ask for images that are both an animal and a natural scene — an otter on a riverbank — and count the fraction of the batch that clears both bars at once. That fraction is an average over the batch, so the theory says the recipe should concentrate — the single best bin should win, not a broad mix. No class label is “animal in nature,” so naming the property gets you nowhere new: asking for animals, asking for nature, or composing the two with Composable Diffusion (the strongest way to compose two conditions) all land near one image in seven. But the audit points to the bins whose images are already both — otters, flamingos — and once you know them, the best move is to draw the whole batch from the single richest one (128 images per seed, ten seeds): how we steered strongly both 95% CI ask for animals (naming) 14.5% [12, 17] ask for nature (naming) 12.8% [11, 15] compose both — Composable Diffusion 13.5% [12, 15] mix 30 audit-chosen both-high bins 45.0% [42, 48] mix the top 5 61.0% [58, 65] the single richest bin (showing, concentrated) 66.5% [64, 69] Naming the property fails (~13%, Composable Diffusion — the strongest way to compose two conditions — included). Showing works, and the more concentrated the recipe the better: thirty audit-chosen bins reach 45%, the top five 61%, the single richest bin 67%. That is the averaging prediction exactly — for an average, the showing recipe should collapse onto the one best bin. It is the extreme of showing: the bin is one the audit chose (the richest, not the average bin), and a knob held inside any one bin reaches only T \sqrt{T} . So the conjunction never needed a spread of bins; it is an averaging goal, and a concentrated recipe — one bin — wins. Figure 9: Claim 3 (averaging goal): how often an image is strongly both animal and natural. Naming the property stays near one in seven; among audit-chosen bins, concentrating the batch scores higher, peaking at the single richest bin. (One bin wins, but you still need the audit to find which bin — that is the showing move. Pick a class at random and crank the knob (pure telling) and you reach only T \sqrt{T} , the within-bin budget; the audit is what points the recipe at the right bin. And which bins pay off is itself forecastable from the audit alone, by a data-side number — the lift — with rank correlation 0.94 to the realized rates.) The same averaging goal on crystals — a structure that is both wide-gap and stable — adds one wrinkle. Three recipes at matched sample size (joint hit = surrogate gap ≥ 3 eV and energy-above-hull ≤ 0.1; six seeds; 95% CIs): how we steered joint hit-rate 95% CI asked naively for both (telling) 2.7% [1.7, 4.3] conditioned on the wide-gap prior (strong telling) 15.5% [12.5, 19.1] drew from wide-gap-and-stable chemistries (showing) 13.2% [10.5, 16.5] As an averaging goal should, one region wins. Mixing chemistries (13.2%) beats a naive request about five-fold (2.7%), but it does not beat the strong single request — conditioning on the model’s own wide-gap prior, 15.5% — the two tie (overlapping CIs, the gap holding at six seeds). Concentrating on the right region is enough; spreading does not help, exactly as for an average. Figure 10: Claim 3 (crystals): the joint of a wide gap and stability — showing beats a naive request about four-fold, but ties a strong single request, because stability (the property Claim 1 found does not carry over) caps both. And the framework says exactly why. Showing does its job on the half it can reach — it produces the most wide-gap structures of any recipe. What caps the joint is the other half: stability sits near one in two for both showing and strong telling. Stability is the property Claim 1 found does not carry over (agreement 0.49) — the model can’t reliably make stable structures however you steer it — so it becomes the binding constraint, and the two recipes converge on it. Showing can choose the chemistry; it cannot make the model honour a property the model never learned to reproduce.

sections.heading:
A goal targeting spread: only showing covers
it
sections.text: Now the goal the theory says genuinely needs showing: a batch that covers both corners of two properties that pull apart — some outputs clearly one, some clearly the other. Score coverage as the smaller of the two corner-fractions, so a recipe scores only if the batch holds both . We committed each prediction before running. Images — a batch with both clean vehicles and clean food (two concepts that genuinely exclude each other, unlike animal-and-nature; 128 images per seed, five seeds): how we steered coverage 95% CI ask for one (telling, one bin) 0.00 [0.00, 0.00] compose both — Composable Diffusion 0.00 [0.00, 0.00] mix a vehicle bin and a food bin (showing) 0.30 [0.27, 0.34] Crystals — a batch spanning the band-gap / dielectric trade-off (genuinely anti-correlated, − 0.54 -0.54 ; pre-registered, three seeds): how we steered coverage 95% CI ask for one (telling, one chemistry) 0.00 [0.00, 0.00] condition on the wide-gap prior 0.02 [0.01, 0.03] mix corner-A and corner-B chemistries (showing) 0.40 [0.35, 0.44] Figure 11: Claim 3 (images): cover a batch with both clean vehicles and clean food. Telling sits in one corner; composing the two conditions collapses to the muddy middle (car-food chimeras, neither a clean car nor a clean meal); only showing — a mix of a vehicle bin and a food bin — puts genuine examples of both in the batch. Figure 12: Claim 3 (crystals): cover the band-gap / dielectric trade-off. Telling lands in one corner, conditioning collapses, only showing spans both corners. Both domains land the same way, and the two scatters tell it at a glance: • Telling sits in one corner. A single bin is all one kind, so coverage is zero by construction. • Composing the two conditions collapses to the muddy middle. Asked for “vehicle and food,” Composable Diffusion makes car-food chimeras — neither a clean car nor a clean meal (92% of the batch in the middle, coverage zero); the crystal conditioning does the same. This is the measured finding: the practitioner’s go-to tool for “both at once” returns the average , not the spread. • Showing covers both corners. A mix of a clean-corner-A bin and a clean-corner-B bin puts genuine examples of each into the batch — coverage 0.30 on images, 0.40 on crystals — the only recipe above zero, by a wide, CI-separated margin. (Precise two-corner mixing is the right recipe: the two cleanest bins cover better than a broad pool, which leaks back toward the middle.) And the gap widens with the number of corners. Two corners is the smallest spread goal. Push to three — a batch that must hold clean vehicles, clean food, and a third clearly distinct kind at once — and the structural gap grows. Count how many corners a recipe covers with real mass (each corner’s fraction CI-separated from zero): telling covers exactly one , its own; composing conditions also covers one (its extra corners are 1–8% leakage, below any honest floor); and showing covers all N N — two of two at N = 2 N=2 , three of three at N = 3 N=3 . The gap, showing minus telling, is N − 1 N-1 , and it widens as you ask for more corners — the disjunctive structure of showing made quantitative: each added corner is one more bin a mix can include and a single named target cannot. (The three properties are mutually uncorrelated, so the corners are genuinely distinct, and the clean N = 3 N=3 test is in images. The richest crystal triple we could form was only about two-dimensional, so it tests coverage but not the N N -scaling cleanly; the magnitude claim rests on the image result.) The two crystal goals split exactly by kind . Wide-gap- and -stable is an averaging goal — you want a high fraction of the batch to be both — so the recipe should concentrate on one well-chosen region, and spreading across many adds nothing; the concentrated recipe tied the strong knob. (It tied low , not high, because stability is the property that does not carry to the model — Claim 1 — so every recipe runs into the same stability ceiling.) The band-gap/dielectric trade-off is a spread goal — the batch must cover both extremes — so only a mix of chemistries reaches it, and there showing wins outright, the same signature as images.

sections.heading: The signature
sections.text: What kind of goal you have sets the shape of the showing recipe. An average over the batch wants one bin : the audit finds the best bin and the recipe concentrates on it — showing at its extreme — capped only when the property does not carry (crystal stability, Claim 1). A goal targeting the batch’s spread wants a mix : covering two corners is something no single bin can do, and composing conditions does not do it either — it returns the average. Both are showing — concentrate for an average, spread for a spread; naming (telling) reaches neither, falling short of the best bin for an average and collapsing to the middle for a spread.

sections.heading:
Claim 4 — Training changes the budget, but in a way you
can
predict
sections.text: Train a model only to reproduce the data and the budget is unchanged. But fine-tuning (filtering, RLHF) deliberately changes which outputs the model favours, so it changes the per-bin numbers the budget is built from — and the claim is that it changes them predictably: recompute the budget from the data and the training recipe, and you have the trained model’s budget without ever sampling it. Plain pretraining changes nothing, so the model’s per-bin averages should match the data’s — and they do, falling on the diagonal: 0.99 agreement for crystal density, and 0.85–0.94 for DiT’s content targets, with the fit tightening as you draw more samples (at the small sample sizes we first used it was noise-limited; the high-spread targets need the most samples and stay loosest). Figure 13: Claim 4: predicted (data) versus observed (model) per-bin average under plain pretraining — the points lie on the diagonal. The two fine-tunes we tested each change the data in a known way; we predict the new per-bin averages from that change, then sample the model and check. Filtering. Keep only outputs above a bar — say, crystals above a density cutoff — and the budget recomputes on the survivors. Predicted versus observed per-bin averages agreed to within 0.03 of a bin width on crystals, 0.002 on images. Guidance. Turning up an image model’s guidance scale should shift the target’s average by a growing amount. Swept over 1, 3, 7, 12 on one class, the average climbed monotonically as predicted — animal score 0.18 → 0.20, brightness 0.52 → 0.57. One case breaks it. Fine-tune a model so hard it abandons its training data and there is nothing left to recompute from. A crystal model fine-tuned aggressively for novelty scored real, held-out structures at −15.1 per token (95% CI [−15.2, −15.0]) — below the −9.7 of random tokens, every held-out structure without exception. For a model like that, drop the data-side prediction and audit the model’s own samples ( Application shows how). Figure 14: Claim 4: how likely the aggressively fine-tuned model thinks real, held-out structures are (per-token score) — below the level for random tokens. It has left its training data behind. (Two more cases — mixing in supervised fine-tuning data, and distilling from a teacher — we leave for later.)

sections.heading: What the evidence shows
sections.text: Four claims from the theory, tested in two fields that share no model, no data, and no code: • The split is exact, and it carries. The budget splits exactly; the split moves as you change the bins; and, for a property the model reproduces faithfully, it carries to the model — and we predicted which properties would carry, in advance, from cheap pre-measurement signals. • Telling and showing reach different budgets, and E / ( E + T ) E/(E{+}T) says which one wins. Telling reweights within a bin, showing across them; at matched effort their reaches differ by E / T \sqrt{E/T} (6.8 / 3.2 / 1.1 on the crystal targets), a ceiling no knob escapes.
