Pushed to the strongest knob each domain allows — best-of-twelve within a fixed chemistry, a learned soft-prompt optimised on the scorer — bins still beat it several-fold on every high- E / ( E + T ) E/(E{+}T) target (crystals 4.8–26× at matched effort, ≈41–800× at the weak deployed tag; images ~3× on semantic content). But with a strong enough knob the low- E / ( E + T ) E/(E{+}T) targets flip — brightness and aesthetic go to the knob — and the budget calls the crossover in advance: above it the range is between bins (showing); below, inside them (a knob). The winning knob wins only by leaving its bin, breaking the bin barrier that defines telling. The key π \pi itself is chosen the same way — pick the cheap partition with the largest data-side E / ( E + T ) E/(E{+}T) (it predicts the realised advantage, rank-correlation 0.88); a low share everywhere means the target is knob-shaped. • The goal’s kind picks the operation. An average over the batch (a high rate, a conjunction “both at once”) is reached by a single bin — telling : naming the properties fails (~one in seven on images), and the best move is to concentrate the batch on the one richest bin (67%); where the property does not carry, even that is capped (crystal stability, a tie — Claim 1). A goal about the batch’s spread — covering two opposed corners — is reached only by a mix , showing : an outright showing win in both domains (coverage 0.30 on images, 0.40 on crystals, predictions committed in advance), where telling gives one corner and composing the two conditions collapses to the average. And the spread gap widens with the number of corners: showing covers all N N , telling one, the gap N − 1 N-1 (clean N = 3 N=3 on images). • Training reshapes the budget, predictably. Recompute it from the data and the recipe — for plain pretraining, filtering, and guidance alike. Two fields that share no model, data, or code land on the same answers — the exact split, the telling/showing asymmetry, the coverage win, the predictable effect of training. That is the strongest sign these are properties of the framework, not of either setup. The clearest agreement is on coverage: showing wins outright in both. The two domains differed in only one place — asking for two things at once, wide-gap and stable, was capped on crystals but not on images — and the framework named the reason in advance: a goal is capped by any property the model fails to reproduce, and stability is exactly that property (Claim 1). What to watch for. This is also the framework’s main limitation, so it is worth collecting in one place. • The budget transfers only for properties the model reproduces well. The one place it transferred weakest was one we predicted: geometry carried almost perfectly (0.99), stability only partly and uncertainly (0.49, wide CI), because the model can’t reliably make stable structures, so there is less for its budget to come through on. • A property that does not carry caps every goal that leans on it. The same weak rung surfaced again in Claim 3: the wide-gap-and-stable goal stalled because its stability half doesn’t carry. The failure to carry over is not a footnote — it sets what any steering method can reach. (The coverage goal, on properties that do carry, was an outright showing win in both domains.) • So when in doubt, audit the model, not the data. If the property you care about may not be reproduced faithfully, score the model’s own outputs rather than the training data. • One boundary is sharper still. A fine-tune can drift so far it leaves its training distribution behind (Claim 4 — the novelty fine-tune scored real structures below random). There the data side predicts nothing at all; sample the model and audit it directly. To put this to work on your own model, see Application ; for the derivations, Theory .

sections.heading:
Reproducing the image-domain
claims
sections.text: The companion repo ( steering/images/ ) ships the audit shadow (132 KB) and the scripts, in two tiers: • Shadow only — no model, no ImageNet, no GPU. verify_dataside.py reproduces Claim 1 (the exact split, the E / ( E + T ) E/(E+T) spectrum, the coarsening E → T E\!\to\!T ) and the Claim 2 data-side bounds, in under a second. • Full regeneration — GPU + public models. claims234.py generates from DiT for the model-side numbers — the realized showing shift, the per-bin averages under plain pretraining, the guidance sweep, the within-bin variety check (use ≥ 50 samples/class for the near-exact fit; the quick default of 8 is noise-limited). claim3_images.py runs the animal-and-nature joint. Not scripted here: the image hard-filter and the aggressive (off-data) fine-tune from Claim 4 — both need the heavier training runs, so the repo ships their results but not a one-command rerun.

sections.heading:
Application — Budget, gap, and how to close
it
sections.text: Say you have a trained generator and you want something particular from it. Brighter images. A batch that covers the whole range from dark to bright. Crystals that are both wide-gap and stable. Or just “more like these forty I picked out.” Some of these you get by telling the model — per-prompt steering, fixing the bin and leaning on the knobs. Others you can only get by showing it: handing over examples and letting their mix steer the batch. This section tells you which, and how to build the recipe when telling isn’t enough. It comes down to one budget and two moves. A cheap key P = π ⁡ ( D ) P=\pi(D) sorts the model’s outputs into bins . For the property L L you want to steer, the data fixes how much room each move has: the spread within a bin is telling’s budget T T ; the spread between bins is showing’s budget E E . Showing works by designing a recipe μ P \mu_{P} over the bins — a distribution over bin labels, like “70% beaches, 30% snow.” Which part you need turns on the kind of goal you have, and there are two. A single number is a level to hit: push one property’s average or rate to a target value. A shape is a pattern in the collection: two properties at once, coverage of a range, or a set you can only point to. (A goal about spread itself — a variance, a diversity score — is a single number too, but it behaves like a shape: no one bin maximizes it, so it lives with the shapes, in §3.) A single number is §2 ; this is reach , the payoff of moving a property further than a knob can. A shape is §3 ; this is expressiveness , steering toward goals a knob cannot articulate. Most readers need one, not both. Either way, start with your per-bin numbers ( §1 ) — off the data, or off the model itself if you don’t have the data.

sections.heading:
1. Get your numbers (the
audit)
sections.text: Everything below runs on an audit (Preliminaries): the three numbers per bin — share w b w_{b} , mean g b g_{b} of L L , spread v b v_{b} of L L . From them: • the within-bin budget T = ∑ b w b ​ v b T=\sum_{b}w_{b}v_{b} — the within-bin spread, averaged over bins (telling’s room); • the between-bin budget E = ∑ b w b ​ ( g b − g ¯ ) 2 E=\sum_{b}w_{b}(g_{b}-\bar{g})^{2} — the spread of the bin means (showing’s room). Both reaches are χ 2 ⋅ budget \sqrt{\chi^{2}\cdot\text{budget}} (derived in Theory ): telling is confined to the within-bin budget, χ tell 2 ​ T \sqrt{\chi^{2}_{\text{tell}}\,T} ; showing reaches the between-bin budget, χ 2 ( μ P ∥ 𝒥 P ) ⋅ E \sqrt{\chi^{2}(\mu_{P}\|\mathcal{J}_{P})\cdot E} , where χ 2 \chi^{2} measures how hard the recipe pushes. In practice per-prompt controls realize only χ tell 2 ≈ 1 \chi^{2}_{\text{tell}}\approx 1 (measured in Evidence ), so telling’s working reach is about T \sqrt{T} — we use that as the practical telling budget below. Showing can push χ 2 \chi^{2} far higher, which is why it reaches so much further. You run the audit one of two ways: Audit 𝒥 \mathcal{J} — you have the training data. Bin each row via π \pi and summarize. (Drop bins with very few rows — say < 5 <5 — so noisy per-bin means don’t inflate E E .) Audit G \mathrm{G} — you only have the model. The bins are fixed by π \pi , so you know them before you sample. Pick a reference recipe μ P ref \mu_{P}^{\text{ref}} to sample under (the training-time mix if you know it, else an even spread over bins, or whatever matches deployment), generate many outputs, and audit those. The identities don’t care whether the outputs came from the data or the model — the model is its own data source. Remember the μ P ref \mu_{P}^{\text{ref}} you used; the budget depends on it. How many to score per bin. π \pi is cheap, so you bin everything and the shares w b w_{b} are exact; ψ \psi is dear, so g b g_{b} and v b v_{b} come from a sample of m m per bin. Sampling few inflates the between-bin budget — bin-mean noise reads as between-bin spread — but by a known amount, E ^ ≈ E + T / m \hat{E}\approx E+T/m . So calculate E ^ − T ^ / m \hat{E}-\hat{T}/m (with T ^ = ∑ b w b ​ v ^ b \hat{T}=\sum_{b}w_{b}\hat{v}_{b} ). Score until that correction is small against E ^ \hat{E} — if bins are small a handful is all that’s needed. An audit is for the L L you are interested in — and how far you can trust the data audit for it depends on how faithfully the model reproduces the data for that property. A generative model is trained to match its data, not to hit any one property, so it reproduces some properties closely and others loosely: a direct readout of the output — an image’s color statistics, a structure’s density — tends to carry, while a property that takes precision the model lacks, or that a separate pipeline scores — stability, an aesthetic rating — can drift. A model can be faithful on one property and loose on another, so judge this per target. Checking that a property carries. When you are unsure, verify it directly. Because ψ \psi is expensive, this costs a second round of scoring, but a cheap one: you are after a systematic gap, not precise per-bin values, so score ψ \psi on a modest sample of G \mathrm{G} ’s outputs in just the bins your recipe leans on — a handful, not all B B . 1. Audit G \mathrm{G} on that sample — sample, bin, score ψ \psi — for the model’s per-bin mean g b ​ ( G ) g_{b}(\mathrm{G}) and spread v b ​ ( G ) v_{b}(\mathrm{G}) . (You already have the data’s g b , v b g_{b},v_{b} from the original audit.) 2. Read two numbers off the comparison: • drift — the typical gap between g b ​ ( G ) g_{b}(\mathrm{G}) and g b g_{b} , i.e. how far the bin means moved; • spread ratio ρ = v b ​ ( G ) / v b \rho=v_{b}(\mathrm{G})/v_{b} — whether within-bin variety came through ( ρ ≈ 1 \rho\approx 1 is faithful). 3. Turn each into a budget error. The drift is how far a showing target lands off: aim a recipe at a shift, and the model misses it by about the drift in the bins it leans on. The spread ratio rescales telling ’s reach — it becomes ρ ​ T \sqrt{\rho\,T} , not T \sqrt{T} , so ρ = 0.8 \rho=0.8 costs about 10%. 4. The verdict, plainly. If the drift is small next to the shift you want and ρ ≈ 1 \rho\approx 1 , the data budget is trustworthy — use 𝒥 \mathcal{J} ’s statistics. If not, don’t lean on it: you computed G \mathrm{G} ’s own g b , v b g_{b},v_{b} in step 1, so build the budget from those instead. This is the test Evidence runs (Claim 1, the carry-over check); the formal drift δ \delta and spread ratio ρ \rho are defined in Appendix A.3. Fine-tuned, not just pretrained? Still fine. A standard fine-tune (filtering, SFT, RLHF) reshapes the data into a predictable 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} . Audit that — the same sums, on reweighted rows (table in Appendix A.1). And if the fine-tune ran so hard it left the base behind, fall back to sampling the model itself, exactly as in the sample-side path above. Worked examples. DiT + ImageNet, target = aesthetic (DiT is a diffusion-transformer image generator; ImageNet its training set): with the ImageNet class as the key (1000 bins), an audit of 100k rows gives a substantial T T (within-class variation from lighting, composition, content) and a substantial E E (some classes are systematically more aesthetic). A crystal generator, target = band gap (trained on a large computed-materials database): with (elements, atom count) as the key, within-chemistry variation gives T T , and between-chemistry mean differences (oxides vs sulfides vs metals) give E E . Evidence has the full tables.

sections.heading: 2. Hitting a target value
sections.text: Say you want your batch’s average aesthetic well above what the model gives by default — or its average brightness, or its rate of “looks like an animal.” These are single-number goals: push the average (or rate) of one property L L to a target. Pin it down as a desired shift Δ \Delta . First, does telling already do it? Telling’s working reach is about T \sqrt{T} — per-prompt knobs (guidance, prompt wording, an adapter) realize only χ tell 2 ≈ 1 \chi^{2}_{\text{tell}}\approx 1 in practice ( Evidence ), so T \sqrt{T} is about as far as they move the mean, whatever the model. Compare it to Δ \Delta : • Δ < T \Delta<\sqrt{T} — telling suffices. Sweep your knobs and you’re done. Example: raise mean aesthetic within one ImageNet class by 0.3. Aesthetic varies a lot inside a class (utilitarian product shots to studio portraits), so T \sqrt{T} comfortably covers 0.3, and a CFG sweep moves the mean there. • Δ ≥ T \Delta\geq\sqrt{T} — a gap by size. Even fully tuned, telling falls short; showing reaches further. Example: raise your batch’s mean “animal-likeness” (a CLIP similarity). That score is mostly fixed by the class, so within any one class telling barely moves it — T \sqrt{T} is small. The only way to lift the batch mean is to draw more from animal-heavy classes. To close a size gap, design a μ P \mu_{P} that lands the batch mean on your target value g ∗ g^{*} (your starting mean plus Δ \Delta ). Two ways. Pool mixing — blend a low and a high pool. Want your batch’s average brightness somewhere in the middle? Take a pool of dark-scene classes (coal mine, night) and a pool of bright ones (beach, snowfield), and turn a single dial α \alpha between them. The math is clean: sample the dark pool with probability α \alpha and the bright one with 1 − α 1-\alpha , and any collection metric linear in the mix interpolates linearly, μ P = α ​ μ P ( 1 ) + ( 1 − α ) ​ μ P ( 2 ) . \mu_{P}=\alpha\,\mu_{P}^{(1)}+(1-\alpha)\,\mu_{P}^{(2)}. What it costs: when the two pools are the bottom and top quantiles of the data (each a fraction q q of the bins by mean), the push is χ 2 ( μ P ∥ 𝒥 P ) = 2 ​ α 2 − 2 ​ α + 1 q − 1 , \chi^{2}(\mu_{P}\|\mathcal{J}_{P})\;=\;\frac{2\alpha^{2}-2\alpha+1}{q}\;-\;1, least at the midpoint, most at the extremes, and halving q q doubles it — so pick the smallest q q that still leaves enough distinct bins to sample without heavy repetition ( q ≳ n gen / n eligible q\gtrsim n_{\text{gen}}/n_{\text{eligible}} ); below that, use min- χ 2 \chi^{2} . This calibrates well in practice. On a crystal generator, mixing a high- Combined pool (rare-earth chemistries, ≈ 0.85) with a broad low one (≈ 0.14) — Combined being a novelty-and-stability benchmark — the dial tracks the target: ask for 0.5 and you get about 0.57, ask for 0.7 and about 0.73, landing within roughly 0.05 of target all the way from 0.2 to 0.8. The reachable range is set by the two pools (here ≈ 0.15–0.85); to go past either end you need a more extreme pool (§4.7). Min- χ 2 \chi^{2} — the gentlest push. χ 2 \chi^{2} is how far your recipe departs from the data’s own mix, and at the same target, less departure is better : a gentler recipe wastes fewer draws on rare bins (§4.6), keeps more of the data’s diversity, and is less likely to stray off-support (§4.5). Pool mixing reaches a middling target the hard way — it piles all the weight onto the two extreme corners. Min- χ 2 \chi^{2} reaches the same target by nudging weight onto the bins whose mean already sits near g ∗ g^{*} , and no further. That recipe — the smallest χ 2 \chi^{2} that still hits g ∗ g^{*} — has a closed form: μ P ​ ( P b ) = 𝒥 P ​ ( P b ) ​ [ 1 + ( g ∗ − g ¯ ) ​ ( g b − g ¯ ) Var 𝒥 ​ ( g b ) ] , g ¯ = 𝔼 𝒥 P ​ [ g b ] . \mu_{P}(P_{b})\;=\;\mathcal{J}_{P}(P_{b})\left[1+\frac{(g^{*}-\bar{g})(g_{b}-\bar{g})}{\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{J}}(g_{b})}\right],\qquad\bar{g}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{J}_{P}}[g_{b}]. For example, to reach g ∗ = 0.65 g^{*}=0.65 it departs only a third as far as pool mixing ( χ 2 = 0.19 \chi^{2}=0.19 vs 0.60 0.60 ) — same target, gentler recipe — and comes out 3–7% more diverse. The catch: for a strict yes/no target it lands a little short ( − 0.20 -0.20 vs − 0.11 -0.11 ), because the bins near g ∗ g^{*} hold a mix of yes and no rows. So: pool mixing for a yes/no target with well-stocked corners; min- χ 2 \chi^{2} for a continuous target, thin corners, or diversity at a fixed target.

sections.heading:
3. Building a shape (when no single number captures the
goal)
sections.text: Some goals aren’t a number at all — they’re a shape in the collection: two properties at once, coverage of a whole range, a set you can only point to. This is the expressiveness the introduction promised — goals a knob cannot articulate, the ones that matter most where naming the target is hardest. Here is why telling can’t reach them. Fix a request z z (a bin plus whatever else you set) and sample: every output comes from one and the same distribution, the model’s conditional G ( ⋅ ∣ z ) \mathrm{G}(\cdot\mid z) . Telling only ever hands you that one distribution. A shape, by contrast, is a blend of distributions — and no amount of pushing turns one distribution into a blend. Only showing, mixing bins through μ P \mu_{P} , builds it. Three common shapes, in order below: (1) a set you can only point to, (2) two properties at once, and (3) a Pareto front to cover. 1. A set you can’t put into words — tacit steering. You’ve pulled together forty images that share a look you can’t name — a washed-out, nostalgic palette, say. You can’t write the prompt, and you have no scorer for the look, but you can point. So hand over the set: read off each image’s bin via π \pi , and the distribution of those bins is your μ P \mu_{P} . Generate from G \mathrm{G} at that μ P \mu_{P} — you never say what the set has in common; the bins they fall in do the steering. With no scorer, you are building μ P \mu_{P} by inferring the target from the examples: the bins they crowd into stand in for the bins that score high. But the recipe only carries which bins your examples came from, not what made each one special inside its bin. If the nostalgic palette depends on the subjects — vintage cars, faded seascapes, old storefronts — the class key sees it: μ P \mu_{P} leans on those classes, and more of them is more of the look. But if the same look is a treatment that can sit on any subject — some “golden retriever” shots washed-out, others crisp, and you picked the washed-out ones — the class key can’t tell the two apart; μ P \mu_{P} just says “golden retriever,” and sampling that class hands you mostly the crisp, average shot, so the nostalgic look is missed. In short: tacit steering reaches a taste the key can read, and misses one the key is blind to. To check this you can do a free pre-check, before you generate. You can’t measure the look — no scorer — but you can ask whether the key sees it at all. Compare the examples’ bin mix μ P \mu_{P} to the data’s 𝒥 P \mathcal{J}_{P} with χ 2 \chi^{2} : if it is no more concentrated than a random draw of the same size — χ 2 \chi^{2} near the floor ( B − 1 ) / n (B-1)/n , for B B bins and n n examples — the key is blind to your taste, and a finer or different key may expose it. A χ 2 \chi^{2} clearly above the floor means the key caught something distinctive: necessary for steering, though not proof it caught your taste rather than something that merely travels with the bins. To keep from reading signal into noise, hold out half the examples and check the concentration survives on the other half. Which bins, not just whether. Finer than that global test, each bin’s lift — its share of your examples over its share of the data — estimates what fraction of that bin clears your bar , with no scorer at all. A small bin that soaks up many of your examples is a near-pure pocket of what you want: a 20-member bin catching ten of your top-percentile picks by chance alone would be a 10 − 27 10^{-27} event. So lean μ P \mu_{P} on the high-lift bins; Appendix B.6 gives the formula and how far to trust it. 2. A and B at once — a joint. Say a photographer wants a portfolio of specific animal-and-lighting pairings — a bright horse, a medium-lit dog, a dim cat. Each pairing is easy on its own, but there’s no clean way to ask a single prompt for “bright horse or medium dog or dim cat” at once. Showing does it directly: hand the model one example of each pairing and let those examples be the recipe — the whole portfolio in a single pass. 3. Cover a Pareto front — front expansion. Often you want two properties at their best together , where pushing one costs the other. Landscape photos that are both vivid and natural-looking, say — crank the color and it turns garish, keep it true and it falls flat — so the best you can do is a front of compromises in between. (Crystals have the same shape: a high band gap and low energy above hull.) You don’t need to know that front in advance: take a rough estimate — a few outputs near it — and build μ P \mu_{P} from their bins. Sampling explores each seed bin’s neighborhood through the model’s own randomness; some outputs push past the seeds, others fill in, and the set’s Pareto volume only grows. Iterate — each round’s outputs seed the next μ P \mu_{P} — and the front expands. Telling pushes one point; showing across seeds expands several at once. Real goals often combine these — a diverse set that must also hit a joint — and the designs stack, so combine them.

sections.heading: 4. Pitfalls
sections.text: Seven practical traps bite even inside the framework’s boundaries (its theoretical edges, where the budget applies at all, are in Theory’s Scope ). One line each below, in three families; the details — numbers and a check for each — are in Appendix E . Getting the audit’s inputs right. • 4.1 Raw-output discipline. Audit raw model outputs; post-processing (DFT relaxation, CFG) is a separate intervention. • 4.2 Label-pipeline drift. Audit labels and evaluation labels from different pipelines produce a systematic offset. • 4.3 Aggressive fine-tune. The closed-form 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} holds only for gentle fine-tunes; once the model has left its data, audit its own samples instead. Where the bound loosens. • 4.4 Heavy-tailed bin means. A few extreme-mean bins make the bound a loose guide, not a sharp ceiling. • 4.5 Off-support μ P \mu_{P} . Mass on untrained bins has no prediction — χ 2 \chi^{2} diverges to flag it. Limits of your pools. • 4.6 Thin corner pools. A tiny corner repeats itself; effective sample size collapses and χ 2 \chi^{2} blows up. • 4.7 Pool reachability. Showing only reaches between your pools; past either end you need a more extreme pool.

sections.heading: 5. End-to-end summary
sections.text: 1. Get your numbers (§1). Per bin: share w b w_{b} , mean g b g_{b} , spread v b v_{b} → budgets T , E T,E . Audit the data, or the model’s own samples if you don’t have the data (report μ P ref \mu_{P}^{\text{ref}} ); fine-tuned model → audit 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} . 2. Single-number goal? (§2) Compare your shift Δ \Delta to telling’s reach T \sqrt{T} . Smaller → telling suffices, sweep the knobs. Larger → a gap by size; design a μ P \mu_{P} to hit your target value — pool mixing, or min- χ 2 \chi^{2} for the gentlest push. 3. Shape goal? (§3) Telling can’t make a shape; show one. Match it: a set you can’t describe → tacit ( μ P \mu_{P} from exemplars); A and B → draw from the bins that hold both; coverage → front expansion. They stack. 4. Generate, measure, verify the result lands inside the predicted bound — and watch the §4 pitfalls. The setup and notation are in Preliminaries ; the derivations in Theory ; the cross-domain corroboration in Evidence .

sections.heading: Related work
sections.text: What is new here is not the posture but the budget. Conditioning a generator on a set of examples — showing , in our terms — is an established move. Reference- and exemplar-conditioned generation (textual inversion, Gal et al. 2023; DreamBooth, Ruiz et al. 2023; IP-Adapter, Ye et al. 2023), retrieval-augmented generation (Blattmann et al. 2022), and few-shot or in-context conditioning all hand a model examples and ask for outputs like them. We claim none of that as our contribution. What this prior work does not ask is the question the budget answers: how far showing can move a target, where that reach comes from, and how it compares to what per-prompt telling can do. Our contribution is the quantitative ceiling — read off the training data before a model is built — not the act of steering by example. Steering a generative model has been studied from many directions. We group the closest threads and say, for each, how the budget relates to it. Throughout we use the paper’s terms: telling is per-prompt steering, showing is choosing the mixture of examples to draw from, and the budget is the split of a target’s variation into a within-bin part (telling’s reach) and a between-bin part (showing’s reach). Full references are at the end of the paper. Controllable generation. A large literature builds knobs for steering — attribute-guided decoding and plug-and-play methods for text (PPLM, Dathathri et al. 2020; GeDi, Krause et al. 2021; prefix- and prompt-tuning, Li & Liang 2021; Lester et al. 2021), and latent-direction editing for images (GAN steerability, Jahanian et al. 2020; InterFaceGAN, Shen et al. 2020). This work asks which interventions exist and how well they work in practice. We ask a prior, quantitative question: given the training data and a way to bin it, how far can any such intervention move a target — a reach you can read off the data before a model is trained. Most of these methods are telling in our terms, and the budget bounds what telling can reach. Guidance at generation time. Classifier guidance (Dhariwal & Nichol 2021) and classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans 2022) push a model harder toward its condition at sampling time. Classifier-free guidance is, underneath, a reweighting of the model’s distribution toward the target — the same closed form as the fine-tunes below — which is why Claim 4 treats it as one of the predictable, training-style changes to the budget rather than a thing apart. Activation- and representation-steering — adding a learned direction to a model’s hidden states to push a behavior (the 2023–2025 line on steering vectors / activation engineering) — is the same move one level down: in our terms a within-bin knob, reaching T T , not E E , unless the added direction changes which bin the output lands in. Fine-tuning and alignment. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (Ziegler et al. 2019; Ouyang et al. 2022), its KL-constrained optimum in closed Boltzmann form (Korbak et al. 2022), and direct preference optimization (Rafailov et al. 2023) all reshape a model’s distribution toward a reward; data filtering and rejection sampling are the blunt limit. The budget absorbs these as closed-form rewrites of the data distribution: recompute the per-bin numbers on the reshaped data and the budget carries — until a fine-tune drives the model off its data, where we stop predicting from the data and audit the model’s own samples instead. Diversity and mode collapse. A long line of work observes that pushing a model to score well costs variety — mode collapse in GANs (Goodfellow et al. 2014; Salimans et al. 2016) — and decomposes generative quality into fidelity and diversity (precision/recall, Sajjadi et al. 2018; Kynkäänniemi et al. 2019; density/coverage, Naeem et al. 2020). The budget gives a structural reason for the trade-off: a reward scores one output at a time, so it reaches only the within-bin budget; the between-bin spread — variety across bins — is reachable only by acting on the mixture of bins, which is showing. Concretely, recall-style diversity is bounded by the between-bin share E / ( E + T ) E/(E{+}T) : a per-output objective, confined to T T , cannot buy the coverage that lives in E E . Mode collapse is what it looks like when an objective uses both parts up. Exemplar and distribution steering. Choosing which bins or examples to draw from — showing — is a reweighting of the data distribution, and the mean shift a reweighting can buy is bounded by a χ²-type divergence between the chosen distribution and the data’s, a standard importance-sampling result (Owen 2013). We make that the reach of showing, paired with the between-bin budget. Bin sampling, selection, and Pareto coverage. The structure underneath showing — allocating a budget of draws across bins — is the subject of several established literatures, whose results we borrow rather than reinvent. The within/between split is one-way ANOVA, with the between-bin fraction η 2 \eta^{2} the standard measure of how much a partition explains; mutual information I ⁡ ( π , L ) I(\pi;L) (Cover & Thomas 2006) is its full-distribution generalization, of which our second-moment budget is the variance approximation. Whether an objective is best served by concentrating draws on one bin or spreading them across many is governed by its curvature: an objective convex in the bin allocation is maximized at a vertex (one bin), a concave one in the interior (a mixture) — the Jensen argument behind exploitation-versus-exploration in multi-armed bandits (Lattimore & Szepesvári 2020). For several properties, the achievable mean vectors are the convex hull of the bin means, and covering the Pareto front is hypervolume maximization (expected hypervolume improvement, Emmerich, Deutz & Klinkenberg 2006); coverage and diversity objectives are submodular, so greedy bin selection is near-optimal (Nemhauser, Wolsey & Fisher 1978; Krause & Golovin 2014); and matching a target output distribution is optimal transport (Peyré & Cuturi 2019). Optimal allocation for estimating a per-bin statistic — what our audit does — is classical stratified sampling (Neyman allocation; Cochran 1977). What none of these ask is our question: they select from a fixed population, whereas we steer a generative model, where the population is what the model produces and the load-bearing step is carry-over — that the model reproduces the data’s bin structure, so a budget read off the data before the model exists transfers to the trained model. The selection mathematics says what an ideal mixture could reach; carry-over is what makes it a statement about a model. Generative models in the two test beds. For images we use a diffusion transformer (DiT, Peebles & Xie 2023) trained on ImageNet (Deng et al. 2009), with a ResNet classifier (He et al. 2016) as the binning key and CLIP/LAION models (Radford et al. 2021; Schuhmann et al. 2022) for the targets. For crystals we use a property-conditioned generator in the family of CDVAE (Xie et al. 2022) and MatterGen (Zeni et al. 2025), trained on data derived from Alexandria (Schmidt et al. 2023), with stability scored by an ML interatomic potential (MACE, Batatia et al. 2022). The two settings share no model, no data, and no code — which is the point: a prediction that holds in both reads as a property of the framework, not of either setup. What the budget adds. Against this background, the contribution is: (1) a model-free audit that reads steerability off the training data alone, before any model exists; (2) a single split that separates two structurally different operations — telling reaches the within-bin part, showing the between-bin part; (3) the χ²-bounded reach of showing; (4) a qualitative asymmetry — some targets are reachable only by reaching across bins, not within one (showing, not telling); and (5) closed-form rewrites that carry the budget through standard fine-tuning, with an honest fallback when they break. The mathematics is standard — the law of total variance for the split (Casella & Berger 2002), Cauchy–Schwarz for the showing bound — assembled into an account of steering rather than newly derived.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: We find that examples are, in general, the more powerful control: a set of examples steers a model far more strongly than its knobs, because a knob is structurally confined to part of what steering can reach. That reach is fixed before the model exists: a target’s movable range splits into a within-bin piece, which knobs reach, and a between-bin piece, which only composing examples reaches. We showed that the split is exact and tested it on two unrelated kinds of model — images and crystals — finding in both that the between-bin piece is usually the larger, so examples win, and by a lot. The advantage is not universal, and the budget says exactly when it is not. That is reach , the measurable payoff. The second is expressiveness : because composing examples unions where a knob can only narrow, it reaches goals a knob cannot articulate — several at once, a Pareto front pushed outward, or a taste an expert can demonstrate but cannot put into words. A familiar family of failures — mode collapse, the alignment tax, reward hacking, the failure to satisfy two requirements at once — share one cause here: each asks a per-output objective such as a per-sample reward to deliver something only a collection holds — variety, coverage, a joint. But those live between bins, beyond the reach of any per-output objective; only showing , which acts across bins, realizes them.

sections.heading: Future work
sections.text: • Training on collections, not rows. Per-example objectives — a likelihood, a per-sample reward — act one output at a time, so they can concentrate the between-bin budget but never enlarge it; the collection-level properties people most want (variety, coverage, joints) are invisible to them. The budget points at the fix: a training signal that scores the batch the model produces, not each sample — a distribution-level objective, the training-side analogue of showing . What such an objective would have to optimize is exactly the between-bin spread the budget measures. • Predicting carry-over from the loss. The budget carries to a model only for properties the training loss effectively constrains; we measure this after the fact. It should be predictable. The loss never sees the object directly — only the representation it scores (tokens, latents) — so a target carries to the extent the loss’s residual error leaves it untouched. A sensitivity analysis of the target against the loss’s under-constrained directions would turn the measured carry-over ladder into a predicted one. (A plain correlation of the target with the loss’s features is a first screen, but not enough: for an invertible representation it is uninformative — the loss’s weighting is what discriminates.) • Discovering the key that exposes a tacit taste. Tacit steering works only when the cheap key sorts the exemplars into bins that track the target (Application §3); when it does not, the examples scatter and χ 2 ( μ P ∥ 𝒥 P ) \chi^{2}(\mu_{P}\|\mathcal{J}_{P}) sits at its random-draw floor. That floor is a scorer-free objective: search a family of keys — coarsenings, learned partitions — for one under which the exemplars concentrate well above it, pulling the taste into the between-bin budget where showing can reach. (Per bin, the lift of Appendix B.6 ranks which bins carry the target; the search is for the key that makes those lifts large.) The open problem is doing it without overfitting — χ 2 \chi^{2} climbs trivially as the bin count approaches the number of examples, and picking the max- χ 2 \chi^{2} key across many candidates invites spurious concentration; held-out validation is a start, a principled penalty the work. It is the same “which representation carries the target” question as the item above, asked from the key side. • The remaining training cases. Two interventions we did not test: mixing in supervised fine-tuning data, and distilling from a teacher. • A milder soft-Boltzmann checkpoint. Our aggressive novelty fine-tune left the data behind; a gentler one would test the closed-form rewrite in the regime where it should still hold.

sections.heading: Reproducibility
sections.text: Every claim is backed by released code and data. The data-side audit reproduces from a 132 KB shadow of per-bin scores with numpy in under a second, no model and no GPU; the model-side checks (carry-over, realized shifts, bins-vs-knobs) run on a single GPU in a few hours. The reproduction repository ships the image and crystal experiment scripts, the shadows, the property scorers, and per-claim verification scripts ( verify_dataside.py , verify_combined.py ); the crystal generator checkpoint is hash-pinned and released separately (weights host), with every scorer’s package and version pinned in the model card. Pre-registered predictions were committed, timestamped, before the audits they forecast, and the commit ordering is checkable in the repository history.

sections.heading: Ethics and broader impact
sections.text: The framework is a measurement and steering tool, not a model: it tells a practitioner, before training, which of two existing operations will move a target property and by how much. Its risks are those of controllable generation generally — the same audit that steers toward a benign property (a material’s stability, an image’s content) steers toward a harmful one, and the between-bin reach it quantifies is the reach an adversary would also have. We see no new capability beyond what prompting and exemplar conditioning already provide; the contribution is understanding why they reach what they reach. The datasets and generators used are public research artifacts, and no human-subjects data was collected.

A model can pass one and fail the other — right bins (high overlap), wrong labels within them (large δ \delta ). Check both. (Recipes in Application .)

sections.heading:
A.4 What the model does — and doesn’t —
change
sections.text: The first objection the budget invites: surely a more expressive model — one that interpolates more richly between training points — produces more variance, so the budget cannot be model-independent. The intuition is right about the outputs and wrong about the budget . A richer model walks the data manifold more densely: it emits a wider, more novel set of outputs D D . But the budget is the variance of a scalar property L = ψ ⁡ ( D ) L=\psi(D) , and richer interpolation fills that property’s distribution in more densely; it does not widen it. Interpolated outputs take property values between the points they interpolate — within the range already present. The only way a model enlarges Var ⁡ ( L ) \mathrm{Var}(L) is to extrapolate — emit outputs whose L L falls outside the training range — which is off support (Part C). So a model’s expressiveness shows up in two places, neither of which touches the budget: • How fully the budget is realized. Finite models drop modes and under-fill bins (contraction, V G < V 𝒥 V_{\mathrm{G}}<V_{\mathcal{J}} ); a richer model contracts less, approaching the data-side budget from below . Expressiveness is less contraction , measured by the within-bin variance ratio ρ = T ⁡ ( G ) / T \rho=\sqrt{T(\mathrm{G})/T} — a consistency check alongside δ \delta ( ρ = 1 \rho=1 match, < 1 <1 contraction, > 1 >1 expansion, the last only off support or under variance-rewarding objectives). • Output diversity itself — coverage, novelty, the size of the produced set — a non-decomposable, collection-level property (Part B). This genuinely depends on the model and is not bounded by Var ⁡ ( L ) \mathrm{Var}(L) ; it lives on a different axis. In one line: richness widens the set of outputs, not the spread of a labeled property.

sections.heading:
A.5 The variance of a steered
collection
sections.text: What is the spread of the L L ’s a recipe μ P \mu_{P} actually produces? The same split applies, weighted by μ P \mu_{P} rather than 𝒥 P \mathcal{J}_{P} , but with the model’s per-bin values, V G ⁡ ( μ ) = ∑ b μ P ​ ( b ) ​ v b ​ ( G ) + ∑ b μ P ​ ( b ) ​ ( g b ​ ( G ) − g ¯ μ ) 2 . V_{\mathrm{G}(\mu)}=\sum_{b}\mu_{P}(b)\,v_{b}(\mathrm{G})+\sum_{b}\mu_{P}(b)\,(g_{b}(\mathrm{G})-\bar{g}_{\mu})^{2}. Because μ P \mu_{P} is a prompt distribution, this threads through the model three times — does it land outputs in the bins you asked for (support overlap), with the per-bin means and spreads the data has ( δ , ρ \delta,\rho , A.3–A.4), and are those bins in support at all? So V G ⁡ ( μ ) V_{\mathrm{G}(\mu)} is exactly forecastable from the audit when the model is faithful on the bins μ P \mu_{P} touches — a checkable condition — and where it is not, the data side cannot answer and you sample G \mathrm{G} (A.2). If μ P \mu_{P} leaves 𝒥 \mathcal{J} ’s support, the bound announces it: χ 2 ( μ P ∥ 𝒥 P ) → ∞ \chi^{2}(\mu_{P}\|\mathcal{J}_{P})\to\infty , so χ 2 ​ E \sqrt{\chi^{2}E} goes vacuous exactly where the audit falls silent. (Note V G ⁡ ( μ ) V_{\mathrm{G}(\mu)} is not capped by V 𝒥 V_{\mathcal{J}} : concentrating μ P \mu_{P} on extreme-mean bins makes the collection more spread than the data — in support; what χ 2 ​ E \sqrt{\chi^{2}E} bounds is the mean shift, not the variance.) A worked edge case. Take 𝒥 \mathcal{J} , remove its two extreme-mean bins to form 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} , and train G \mathrm{G} on 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} — then prompt for exactly those removed bins. Since they carry no mass in 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} , χ 2 ( μ P ∥ 𝒥 P ′ ) → ∞ \chi^{2}(\mu_{P}\|\mathcal{J}^{\prime}_{P})\to\infty and the bound is vacuous: the framework makes no claim. Whether the spread of G ⁡ ( μ ) \mathrm{G}(\mu) exceeds even V 𝒥 V_{\mathcal{J}} is then entirely up to how G \mathrm{G} extrapolates — outward, and it overshoots 𝒥 \mathcal{J} ; back onto its own support, and it stays under 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} . The framework predicts neither; it flags the regime (the diverging χ 2 \chi^{2} ) and sends you to measure G \mathrm{G} . The example also fixes which distribution to audit: G \mathrm{G} ’s reference is 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} , the data it actually saw — auditing against the original 𝒥 \mathcal{J} would forecast a reach G \mathrm{G} has no in-support way to deliver.

sections.heading:
B.1 The combinatorial
trap
sections.text: The AND/OR observation of the Intro acquires teeth here. Telling is conjunctive: a bin specified by discrete property labels is an intersection of label values, and the number of such bins explodes exponentially in the number of properties. In practice most intersections are unrepresented in training, many were never labeled, and many interesting regions fall between named label values. So the fraction of Var 𝒥 ​ ( L ) \mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{J}}(L) that label-based telling can actually address shrinks as property dimensionality grows. Showing has no such problem: a set of examples points at the bins that matter and needs no combinatorial coverage.

sections.heading:
B.2 Telling has narrow
reach
sections.text: Confined to the within-bin budget T T : telling reweights within a bin, so its reach is χ tell 2 ​ T \sqrt{\chi^{2}_{\text{tell}}\,T} — and since per-prompt controls realize only χ tell 2 ≈ 1 \chi^{2}_{\text{tell}}\approx 1 in practice ( Evidence ), that working reach is about T \sqrt{T} . Stacking tokens at one bin sharpens the bin-conditional but cannot leave the bin or enlarge T T — telling only moves L L around within a bin’s existing spread. This is the precise form of “telling can only narrow.”

sections.heading:
B.3 Decomposable vs non-decomposable
metrics
sections.text: Collection-level metrics split into decomposable ( Φ = ( 1 / n ) ​ ∑ i ϕ ⁡ ( D i ) \Phi=(1/n)\sum_{i}\phi(D_{i}) ) and non-decomposable (properties of the joint distribution of the output set). Telling can partly substitute for showing on decomposable metrics; on non-decomposable ones — set diversity, coverage, joint targets — it cannot, because there is no single-sample quantity to push. By curvature (the full table). A goal is a property of the batch; showing shifts weight across bins via the recipe μ \mu (all on one bin = concentrate , many bins = spread ), and the goal’s curvature decides which — convex (peaks at one bin) → concentrate, concave (peaks at a blend) → spread. Both are showing; telling (within-bin knobs) only refines the result inside whatever bin you land in. The two non-obvious rows: variance is concave because blending bins adds the between-bin term, Var ⁡ ( λ ​ R 1 + ( 1 − λ ) ​ R 2 ) = λ ​ Var 1 + ( 1 − λ ) ​ Var 2 + λ ⁡ ( 1 − λ ) ​ ( μ 1 − μ 2 ) 2 \mathrm{Var}(\lambda R_{1}+(1{-}\lambda)R_{2})=\lambda\mathrm{Var}_{1}+(1{-}\lambda)\mathrm{Var}_{2}+\lambda(1{-}\lambda)(\mu_{1}-\mu_{2})^{2} , so spread is a showing goal; distribution-matching minimizes a divergence (a quantity that bends upward), a concave goal whose best is a mixture. The raw extremes are set by a single point and do not sort by curvature; their smooth proxies do. Multiple properties (the Pareto front). With N N properties each bin is a point in ℝ N \mathbb{R}^{N} and a recipe’s reachable means fill the convex hull. The goal — span the Pareto front of non-dominated trade-offs — is a coverage goal, so by the curvature rule it wants a mixture. This tilts toward showing as N N grows: each added property is another corner the one ellipsoid must reach while its reach does not grow, so by N ≳ 5 N\gtrsim 5 specialist bins are almost always needed (a lower bound: one bin plus one specialist per property the best bin cannot reach). Coverage is submodular, so greedy specialist selection is within 1 − 1 / e 1-1/e of optimal; the exact objective is the expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI; Emmerich, Deutz & Klinkenberg 2006).

sections.heading: B.4 Five cases
sections.text: Each opens on the concrete instance, then states the structural reason — always the same: telling is confined to within-bin room T T (reach χ tell 2 ​ T \sqrt{\chi^{2}_{\text{tell}}\,T} , with χ tell 2 ≈ 1 \chi^{2}_{\text{tell}}\approx 1 ); showing reaches between-bin room ( χ 2 ⋅ E \sqrt{\chi^{2}\cdot E} ). Joint targets. Image: high-aesthetic AND animal-like. Crystal: wide-bandgap AND on-hull. Telling both narrows the conditional toward zero mass — the cleanest failure. But some bins already contain joint examples, and a μ P \mu_{P} on those bins reaches the joint by composition. Tacit targets. Image: a cloud of pictures you find compelling. Crystal: materials you recognize as promising. The essence of showing: you cannot articulate the shared property, so there is no token to set. The exemplar set is the specification; the bin distribution it induces does the steering, and G \mathrm{G} draws more without anyone saying why. Non-rectangular property spaces. Crystal: the realizable manifold is not a box in property coordinates. Telling tries to reach off-manifold corners and fails; a μ P \mu_{P} on bins that populate those corners reaches them. Pareto-front exploration. Both: cover a trade-off front in two properties L A , L B L_{A},L_{B} , not a point. Telling gives one point at a time; a μ P \mu_{P} weighted along the front covers it by construction — a collection-level target with no single-sample analogue. (This is the one place two properties appear together; elsewhere a single L L suffices.) Properties without articulable tokens. Both: diversity, novelty, set statistics. Telling has no token to manipulate; the choice of μ P \mu_{P} always exists as a knob.

sections.heading:
B.5 Two honest failure modes of
showing
sections.text: Showing is not magic, and the formalism says where it strains. 1. The density problem. “More like these” assumes G \mathrm{G} ’s geometry agrees with what made the exemplars appealing. It may not — G \mathrm{G} does not know why the set was chosen, so “near in G \mathrm{G} ’s sense” can drift from “appealing in the user’s sense.” This is the gap between bin membership and the within-bin detail T T the user may actually care about. 2. The distributional-shape problem. “Variety along several axes at once” — exemplars define a cloud but not its shape along specific axes. The resolution is in the formalism: treat the exemplar set as a distribution , not a set. Want more big dogs? Supply more big-dog exemplars. The distribution of inputs shapes the distribution of outputs; the desired variety is curated in, not articulated. Both fall straight out of the budget decomposition, and naming them sharpens the boundary of what showing buys rather than weakening it.

B.6 What the exemplars tell you about a bin — the

sections.text: In tacit steering (Application §3) you build μ P \mu_{P} from exemplars with no scorer. How much does that reveal about the unmeasured target? Assume only that the expert picks among the best — selection probability rises with L L , at overall rate s s (e.g. s = 0.01 s=0.01 for a top-centile bar). Let q b q_{b} be the fraction of bin b b ’s members that clear the bar. (Sampling new outputs from these bins then inherits the usual carry-over of §A.2 — G \mathrm{G} must reproduce the bin’s L L -distribution.) Worked example. sections.heading:
C. Scope — the full boundary
statement
sections.text: Theory §5 summarizes the boundary; here it is in full. None of what follows is a hedge — each is a clean edge of a sharp claim, and almost every one comes with a cheap check that tells you which side of it you are on. What the framework claims. The budget and its two reaches bound the mean shift of a labeled property L L that can be had by selection — choosing which of the model’s behaviors to sample, whether by telling (within a bin) or showing (across bins). The claims hold when the model’s output distribution matches 𝒥 \mathcal{J} on the bins in play: at the MLE limit within support, or — after a standard fine-tune — against the closed-form 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} of A.1. Where it stops — and what to do instead. • Off support. If the model is pushed to extrapolate, or μ P \mu_{P} puts mass on bins absent from training, the data-side audit has nothing to say. The signal is built in: χ 2 ( μ P ∥ 𝒥 P ) → ∞ \chi^{2}(\mu_{P}\|\mathcal{J}_{P})\to\infty and support overlap drops. There, drop the forecast and audit G \mathrm{G} empirically (A.2). • Mean, not range. We bound the mean shift (and account for variances); we never claim the literal extremes. A model can produce an L L past anything in training by extrapolating — off-support behavior, not a broken claim, because the min–max range was never the quantity. • Realization (the model can fall short or run over). The budget is a data-side forecast . A finite model usually falls short by contracting ( ρ < 1 \rho<1 , mode-dropping); off support or under variance-rewarding objectives it can expand ( ρ > 1 \rho>1 ) past the reach. The diagnostics ρ \rho and δ \delta (A.3–A.4) say which. • The spread of a steered batch. V G ⁡ ( μ ) V_{\mathrm{G}(\mu)} is not capped by Var 𝒥 ​ ( L ) \mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{J}}(L) — concentrating μ P \mu_{P} on extreme-mean bins makes a batch more spread than the data, in support. The reach bounds the mean shift, not the batch variance (A.5). • Heavy-tailed bin means. The showing reach is a second-moment bound; a few bins with extreme means can carry the mean shift past it. Inspect the tail before quoting it tight (Application §4.4). • Set-level targets. The reaches bound a mean . Non-decomposable, collection-level properties — diversity, coverage, joint hit-rate — are a different object (B.3); telling and showing still differ there, but the closed-form bound is for the mean. • Leaving the selection regime. Operations that don’t work by selection — gradient search on the output at inference time, say — can push L L past the budget. They escape it only by leaving the regime where training data predicts behavior: a trade, not a free lunch. • Multi-property L L . We work one property at a time; several at once generalize through the law of total covariance (and appear together only in the Pareto case, B.4). • Non-iid generation complicates the concentration arguments for collection-level stability; the reaches hold in expectation, and a particular batch may deviate. Practical (not theoretical) caveats — raw-output discipline, label-pipeline drift for learned-classifier labels, finite-sample audit noise — are in Application §4 (with the details in E ).

sections.heading:
D. Why variance, not range (the methodological
choice)
sections.text: Theory §1 uses Var 𝒥 ​ ( L ) \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{J}}(L)} as the unit of reach and notes in passing that the range max ⁡ L − min ⁡ L \max L-\min L would be the wrong choice. In full: mean-shift reach under controlled reweighting scales with variance, not range (that is what the Cauchy–Schwarz step gives); range has no clean within-bin / between-bin identity, so it cannot be split into the two per-operation budgets at all; and range is fragile — set by a single extreme row, sensitive to sampling luck, and routinely exceeded by G \mathrm{G} ’s own outputs when the model interpolates. Variance is the stable data-side quantity. (Worked argument in crystal_example.md .)

sections.heading:
E. Practical pitfalls — the
details
sections.text: The seven traps listed in Application §4 , each with its numbers and the check to run (numbered to match §4; cross-references point back to Application).

sections.heading:
4.1 Audit raw outputs, not post-processed
ones
sections.text: Run DFT relaxation on a crystal model’s outputs before auditing them and the gap between prediction and observation jumps about fourfold. The reason: the audit describes what the model puts out, and relaxation — like CFG for images, or any refinement network — is a separate step with its own effect on the distribution. So audit and measure the raw outputs (pre-relaxation structures, images at CFG=1), and treat any post-processing as its own intervention.

sections.heading:
4.2 Watch for label drift between audit and
check
sections.text: On DiT at CFG=1, the LAION aesthetic scorer rates the generated images about 0.44 points lower than it rated the training images — even though the model’s outputs otherwise match the data. That gap isn’t the model; it’s the scorer reacting differently to generated images than to real ones. (Brightness and CLIP-similarity labels, crisply defined, show essentially none of it.) The general trap: your prediction uses the label values recorded in the data ( g b g_{b} ), but your check uses whatever your evaluation pipeline computes — produce the two differently and a systematic offset appears. Crystal example: evaluating Combined , the training stability label is a DFT energy-above-hull, but the benchmark recomputes it with an ensemble of machine-learned potentials; the two disagree at the stability boundary by ∼ 10 \sim 10 pp, producing a roughly constant offset between predicted and observed Combined. Either recompute the audit with the evaluation pipeline’s labels (expensive) or report the observed-vs-predicted gap separately (the honest two-step framing). Structural labels measured the same way on both sides (brightness, density) don’t have this issue.

sections.heading:
4.3 When a fine-tune is too aggressive to audit from
data
sections.text: A crystal model fine-tuned hard toward novelty drifted so far that it almost never produced the structures its base did — it scored held-out base structures below random chance (per-token log-probability ≈ − 17 \approx-17 , versus ≈ − 9.7 \approx-9.7 for uniform). At that point there’s no use computing the budget from the original data: the model no longer resembles it. The shortcut for a fine-tuned model — rewriting it as a reweighted copy of the data (the 𝒥 ′ \mathcal{J}^{\prime} trick, Appendix A.1) — works only while the fine-tune is gentle enough that the model still mostly produces things the data contained. How to check: sample a few hundred outputs under your deployment recipe and see what fraction land in training bins. High ( ≥ 90 % \geq 90\% ): the data-based audit holds. Low ( < 80 % <80\% ): audit the model’s own samples instead (§1, sample-side).

sections.heading:
4.4 A few extreme bins make the bound a loose
guide
sections.text: The showing bound averages squared deviations across bins, so it goes slack when a few bins sit far out from the rest — a heavy tail. A recipe that leans on those few bins can move the mean by much less than the averaged bound suggests, so the bound stops being a tight prediction and becomes only a ceiling. On ImageNet, brightness has exactly this shape (a handful of very bright classes), and across our concentration sweep its realized shift stayed well under the bound at every level — the ceiling held, but it was loose, rising far faster than the reach it was supposed to predict. The averaging cuts the other way too: with a heavy enough tail it carries no guarantee the realized shift won’t run over, so don’t treat it as exact. How to check: before quoting the bound as tight, look at the spread of bin means; if a handful dominate, read it as a loose guide, not a sharp number.

sections.heading:
4.5 Recipes that wander off the training
data
sections.text: Build a μ P \mu_{P} that puts real weight on bins the training set never contained, and the budget has nothing to say there — it was computed from data that doesn’t cover that ground. Usefully, the χ 2 \chi^{2} factor announces this itself: it blows up as μ P \mu_{P} puts mass where the data had none, so the bound χ 2 ​ E \sqrt{\chi^{2}E} goes vacuous right at the edge of support. Fix: whenever you build a μ P \mu_{P} , check how much of its mass lands on training bins; if a meaningful share is off-support, drop those bins and renormalize, or flag those outputs as outside the framework.

sections.heading:
4.6 Thin corner pools repeat
themselves
sections.text: Aiming at a target g ∗ = 0.35 g^{*}=0.35 from a corner of only 20 bins (64 rows), a pool-mixing design drew 35 prompts but got only 87 distinct ones out of 100 — the same few bins kept coming up. With so little to draw from you effectively have far fewer independent samples (here 73.5, not 100), and the push χ 2 \chi^{2} shoots up to 52.3, two orders of magnitude above a healthy pool — predictable from χ 2 ≈ 1 / q − 1 \chi^{2}\approx 1/q-1 . How to check: compute the floor q ≳ n gen / n eligible q\gtrsim n_{\text{gen}}/n_{\text{eligible}} ; below it, switch to min- χ 2 \chi^{2} , which borrows from the middling bins to recover independent samples, at some cost in precision.

sections.heading:
4.7 You can only reach as far as your
pools
sections.text: Showing steers between the extremes your pools provide. With a high pool at Combined ≈ 0.85 and a broad low one at ≈ 0.14, the reachable range is about 0.15 to 0.85 : ask for 0.1 and you saturate at ~0.15, ask above 0.85 and there is nothing to mix toward. To widen the range you need a more extreme pool — if the data holds one. (More deeply, a real model carries its data’s statistics only in the ideal limit (Theory, Claim 1), so its reachable range can sit inside the data-side bound; past that, the bound over-promises.) How to check: measure your two anchor pools’ scores first — that bracket is your range.
