Turn one as hard as you like and, past a point, it stops moving the property you care about. We find that ceiling is not a shortcoming of the model but a budget , set by the training data before the model is trained: a property’s movable range splits in two — the part a knob can reach, and a second, significant part that only examples — concrete instances of what you want more of — can reach. That second part is usually much larger, but not always, and the same budget says so in advance. Reaching that second part takes a different move: instead of turning a knob, you show the model examples, composed from what it already learned rather than added to its training. A cheap audit of the training data measures the budget; we give a recipe for building the example set that reaches all of it. This buys two things a knob can’t. Reach: it moves a property across the whole budget, not just the part a knob reaches. Expressiveness: it steers toward targets you can only specify by example — including ones you can’t put into words. We turn these into a handful of falsifiable claims and verify them in two unrelated domains, image and crystal-structure generation — marking where a knob is enough, and where only examples will do. Introduction — Steering with knobs, and steering by example Suppose you have a generative model and you want it to lean a certain way — images with the feel of nature photography, crystal structures with a wider band gap. You reach for the controls: a prompt, a guidance scale, a property tag. Push them to their limit and they still carry the output only so far — the property you are steering settles well short of where you wanted it, and leaning harder does nothing. There is a more powerful move, and it is not a better knob. It is a change in what you hand the model . Instead of working the controls, you show it: a set of examples, and the instruction “more like these.” The examples are drawn from what the model already learned — you are not adding to its training or retraining it, only choosing which of its own material it works from. We find that this is the more powerful and more expressive way to steer — and, more surprisingly, that the gap between the two is not incidental but budgeted : how far each can move a property is fixed, before the model is trained, by the data it learned from. That budget is the spine of the paper. Examples play two different roles in it. The training data sets how big each part of the budget is — settled before the model exists. The examples you show at steering time are how you reach the part a knob cannot. The rest of this section previews the split, names the two operations, shows why the part a knob misses is the part people most often want — and ends on the targets an expert can recognize but cannot put into words. Telling and showing So far we have two handles: knobs and examples. To say precisely how far each reaches, we need names for the two acts , not just the two things you hold. Turning a knob is telling . Handing over examples — “more like these” — is showing . These two acts have a precise structural difference, and it is the crux of the paper. Telling is conjunctive. Every label specification is an intersection: object = dog AND brightness = high AND size = large narrows the output set on each conjunct. You can only cut away. There is no natural way to say or — to ask for big bright dogs or small dark cats — without enumerating the union explicitly, which requires knowing the union in advance. Showing is disjunctive. An exemplar set can hold big bright dogs and small dark cats and medium fluffy spaniels at once, and “more like these” finds what is interesting about the collection without anyone naming the union. The or lives in the diversity of the set. The AND/OR observation. Telling can only narrow — it intersects. Showing can union — the disjunction lives in the spread of the examples, and never has to be articulated. That contrast — telling narrows, showing unions — is why showing reaches what telling cannot. The rest of the paper makes it precise, shows exactly how far each posture reaches, and tests the prediction in two unrelated domains. A budget on what steering can reach Behind the AND/OR difference is something you can measure. Telling is the familiar operation: decide what you want and lean on the controls — the guidance dial, a descriptive token, an adapter — nudging the distribution one request at a time. Showing is the other: hand over a set of examples and let them shape a whole batch, never saying what they have in common. Here is what separates them. A cheap label — the class of an image, the chemistry of a crystal — sorts a model’s outputs into groups; call each a bin . Any property you care about, like brightness or a crystal’s band gap, varies two ways: within bins (golden retrievers differ in brightness) and between bins (a beach averages brighter than a wine cellar). Those two pieces add up to all the variation there is — and telling , working inside the bin you asked for, reaches only the within-bin part, while showing , choosing which bins the batch is drawn from, reaches the between-bin part. Each piece is a budget — a ceiling on how far that operation can move the property — fixed by the training data before the model is built. Preliminaries makes this precise. One question this raises: if the budget is set by the data, doesn’t that write the model out of the story? No — a stronger model produces a denser, more novel set of outputs, but that is a richer set, not a wider spread of any one property; we make the distinction precise later. So the two reach genuinely different ground. Much of what people actually want — outputs that meet two conditions at once, real variety across a batch, a preference you cannot put into words — lives in the part telling cannot reach. That is the ground showing covers. Steering toward what you can’t name Reach — moving a property further than a knob can — is the measurable payoff, and most of the paper is about it. There is a second payoff, and it matters most exactly where naming the target is hardest. A materials scientist scrolling a list of candidate structures stops on one: that one looks promising. Pressed for a reason, they hesitate — the judgment is fast and reliable, the justification slow and partial. A film editor who keeps one take in ten is in the same position: the cut hangs together, but the rule that chose those takes resists being written down. This is the ordinary condition of expertise, not an edge case; Polanyi’s phrase is we know more than we can tell. Every knob asks the expert to tell anyway — to name the target in the model’s vocabulary before it can be pursued. Showing does not. The specification lives in the examples themselves, so you can steer toward a taste you can demonstrate but not articulate: keep the ten candidates you would have kept, hand them over, and ask for more like them. And because showing composes by union — the examples may disagree, and “more like these” finds what they share without anyone naming it — it reaches tastes, trade-offs, and combinations no single named target captures. This expressiveness is what the budget’s between-bin part pays for; we return to it, and to its uses, in Application . Why this matters even if you never use exemplars You might expect the telling / showing split to matter only when you have exemplars in hand. It reaches further than that: it sits underneath some of the most familiar frustrations in generative modeling. Here is why. Almost every way we train or tune a model — fitting it to data, optimizing it against a reward, nudging it toward preferences — works one output at a time , pushing each toward “better.” Tuning output by output can sharpen each one, but it cannot build variety — because variety is not a property of any single output. It is a property of the whole collection , and the collection is exactly the ground showing governs and telling never reaches. So the harder you tune for quality, the less variety comes back. Anyone who has fine-tuned a model and watched it turn repetitive has met this. The variety did not evaporate for no reason: output-by-output tuning can only narrow it, never produce it; the variety lives between bins, and only showing reaches it. The field already has names for the symptoms, usually treated one by one: a model collapsing onto a handful of outputs ( mode collapse ); a tuned model that answers well but has lost its range (the alignment tax ); a model that games its score by overproducing one safe thing ( reward hacking ); a model that can satisfy two requirements on their own but not together ( compositional generalization ). One cause sits under all four: each asks output-by-output tuning to deliver something it structurally cannot — variety, coverage, a joint, all properties of the collection rather than of any single output — and that tuning can only concentrate, never supply it. Reaching them takes a move across the collection, which is what showing names. Alongside each phenomenon’s familiar drivers, Theory makes that tie explicit. The lost variety, it turns out, is part of the budget itself — used up by tuning, and put back only by acting on the collection. Evidence across two domains We do not just argue this; we test it, in two fields that share no model, data, or code — a diffusion model trained on ImageNet, where the bins and the steering are easy to see, and a generator of crystal structures, where an expert routinely flags a promising candidate without being able to say why. This section previews what we find; Evidence has the numbers. Examples are the more powerful control in general — and the budget says exactly when. On crystals, choosing which chemistries a batch is drawn from moves a target tens to hundreds of times more than the model’s own “high band gap” dial — and still several times more when we replace that dial with the strongest within-chemistry knob we can build. On images, choosing which classes moves the semantic targets a guidance dial can barely touch. The advantage is not universal, and the framework predicts when knobs are powerful enough. In the image domain, we show that knobs are sufficient to move brightness, and can be made to improve aesthetics too — but only by drifting across bins. Examples express what a knob cannot. Ask for a batch that holds two opposing kinds at once — clean vehicles and clean food, or crystals spanning a materials trade-off — and a knob gives you one kind, or a blurred average of the two; only composing examples puts genuine instances of both in the batch. And the budget is real, not just bookkeeping. The split into the two parts is exact by construction. Properties aligned with the model’s training goals carry through to the trained model; some do not — and we show you can predict which will. Most of the checks are cheap to verify. The budget itself is a variance calculation on training data — it runs on a laptop. Only the last step, confirming that a real model behaves the way the budget predicts, has to generate samples; even that fit on a single machine with a GPU in a few hours. What the paper contributes The rest of the paper turns the tell/show idea into something you can compute, test, and use. The central claim is this: the steerable mean-shift of a labeled property splits into a telling part and a showing part, both computable from training data before the model exists — and this reveals which targets telling cannot reach. Five contributions follow, in the order they arrive: • The distinction itself, made precise — telling and showing as two operations, and the AND/OR observation that fixes what each can express. • A budget you can compute in advance — the exact accounting that splits a property’s variation into a within-bin part (what telling reaches) and a between-bin part (what showing reaches), with a ceiling on each, from training data alone. • A unifying lens on four familiar problems — mode collapse, the alignment tax, reward hacking, and the failure to compose requirements, read as a single mismatch: telling sent to do a showing job. • Evidence in two unrelated fields — images and crystals — that composing examples is, in general, the stronger lever: it moves a target several-fold further than the strongest knob we could build wherever the budget is mostly between-bin, and it is the only way to cover two opposed properties in one batch (which neither prompting nor composing conditions can do). The budget also calls the cases where examples are not the move — the low-level scalars (image brightness, aesthetic) whose range sits mostly inside the bins, where a strong knob wins; a goal that is merely a batch average, which a single well-chosen category already meets — and the one place nothing helps: a property the model reproduces too poorly for any recipe to reach. • A recipe — even when you can’t name the target. When telling falls short, we show how to choose which categories to draw from: if you can score the target, find the categories that rank high on it in the training data. If you can’t — a preference you can only point to — use a handful of samples you like to choose categories for you by picking the categories they fall into. What’s new, and what isn’t. Steering by example is not itself new — example- and reference-conditioned generation take similar approaches. What’s new here is the articulation of the budget: a quantitative account, read from the training data, of how far telling and showing can each reach. (Related Work places it among these.) When a knob is enough Examples are the stronger lever, but not everywhere — and the same budget that says when they win says when they are not worth the trouble. There are two such cases, each with a cheap check: • The knob already reaches. When little of a property’s variation sits between bins — its between-bin share is small — and a knob drives it directly, a knob is enough. Check: measure that between-bin share from the data; if it is small, the knob has the room. (Image brightness is the one such case we found.) • The model doesn’t reproduce the property. The budget is read off the data, so it transfers only to properties the model makes faithfully; for one it does not, no recipe reaches it. Check: audit a sample of the model’s own outputs against the data. In short: measure the budget first, and let it tell you whether to reach for examples at all. Roadmap Preliminaries sets up the shared language in two pages — the bins, the two operations, the two budgets — and sends you on. Theory derives the two bounds, shows how the choice of exemplars scales what showing can reach, states the four falsifiable claims, and closes by connecting them back to the phenomena above. Evidence tests the claims in both fields. Application turns it into a recipe: measure your budget, measure how far telling already gets you, and — if a gap remains — read its shape to choose how to close it. Preliminaries — the cheap key and the expensive target The introduction named two moves — telling and showing — and a budget that splits between them. This section makes all three precise: the bins, the two moves, and the two budgets. Everything after is built from them. A generative model hands you a stream of outputs, and you want to steer it — more of some kinds, fewer of others. Some of what makes an output desirable is cheap to read: the class of an image, the elements in a crystal. What you usually care about is expensive: whether an image looks good takes a second trained model, or a person, to judge; a crystal’s band gap — the number that decides whether it is a useful semiconductor — takes a physics simulation that can run for hours. These two reads — the cheap one and the expensive one — are most of the notation in this section. • The cheap read is a label P P , from a function π \pi (the classifier, the formula-reader): P = π ⁡ ( D ) P=\pi(D) for an output D D . • The expensive property is L L , from a function ψ \psi (the aesthetic scorer, the band-gap simulation): L = ψ ⁡ ( D ) L=\psi(D) . The one idea to carry: P P is a key, not a measurement. It sorts outputs into groups: every golden-retriever picture into one, every table-salt crystal into another. Call each group a bin . The whole paper is about steering the expensive L L by choosing how we work with the cheap bins P P gives us. Bins Run π \pi over a pile of outputs and it drops each into a bin — one bin per distinct label. For the image model there is a “golden retriever” bin, a “ladybug” bin, one per class. For the crystal model π \pi reads (elements, atom count), so there is a (Si, O; 6) bin, a (Mg, O; 2) bin, and so on. With B B distinct labels there are B B bins, and P b P_{b} is the label of bin b b . (A real request carries more than the key — a guidance scale, a style token — the knobs of the introduction. P P is the part this paper turns on, so we fold those into “the controls” and set them aside for now; they return below as telling .) What the model produces What is the model trained to make? More of whatever it learned from — and it is random : ask it once and you get one output; ask again, same request, and you get a different one. A request doesn’t pin down an output, it pins down a spread of outputs. What that spread looks like is fixed by the data the model trained on. So name that data: 𝒥 \mathcal{J} is the distribution of your training set. Train on ImageNet and 𝒥 \mathcal{J} is ImageNet’s distribution; train on a different collection and 𝒥 \mathcal{J} is different. The framework is computed relative to the data you used: your budget for a property is set by your training set. We never need 𝒥 \mathcal{J} itself — a distribution over whole images, or whole crystals. We need only its shadow on ( P , L ) (P,L) : pass each output through the cheap label P P and the property L L , and keep a few numbers per bin. That shadow is all the machinery ever touches, and it is concrete — just statistics of your data. The working picture Now take the expensive property L L — the band gap — and look at how it varies across the bins. It varies two ways: • within a bin, the (Si, O; 6) crystals do not all share one band gap; • between bins, the averages differ — silicon oxides sit near 1 eV, magnesium oxides up near 7 eV. So picture B B columns, one per bin, each a cloud of L L values — every cloud has some spread, and the columns sit at different heights. One output’s band gap is one dot in one column. Figure 1: Each bin is a column of L values: every column has some spread (the within-bin variation) and sits at a height (the bin’s average). Some bins are tight and high, others wide and low. (Schematic — illustrative numbers, not measured data.) Each column is a bin; the dots are the L L values in it. A column’s spread is the within-bin variation; its height is the average. This is the picture to keep for the whole paper. (The image model looks the same: each class is a column, brightness varies within a class, and some classes — beaches — average brighter than others — coal mines.) The audit The working picture reduces to three numbers per bin, and producing them is one fixed procedure — an audit : take a set of outputs, sort each into its bin via P P — cheap, so you bin them all — then score the expensive L L on a handful of outputs from each bin (few, because ψ \psi is dear, but enough to pin down the bin’s average and spread), and record, per bin, • its share w b w_{b} — the fraction of outputs that land in it; • its height g b g_{b} — the average L L in it; • its spread v b v_{b} — how much L L varies inside it. Those three numbers per bin are the audit’s output — its shadow on ( P , L ) (P,L) — and the entire input to everything that follows. Because π \pi is cheap but ψ \psi dear, the shares w b w_{b} come out exact — you bin everything — while the heights and spreads are estimates from the scored handful: a few per bin are enough for the targets steering cares about, more when L L varies mostly within bins. Application gives the rule for choosing the count, and the correction for sampling so few. You can run the very same procedure on two different sets of outputs: your training data ( audit 𝒥 \mathcal{J} ) or a batch of the model’s own samples ( audit G \mathrm{G} ). From here on those two terms mean precisely this — the binning and the three numbers — and the rest of the paper uses them without re-explaining. Two ways to steer Say you want brighter images. Here are the two moves the introduction named, now made precise — and the rest of the paper turns on the difference between them. • Telling ( per-prompt steering ). Work within one bin — say “golden retriever” — and lean on the controls: turn up the guidance dial, add the token “bright”, attach an adapter. You shift that bin’s outputs toward its brighter end. In the picture: you stay in one column and pull its dots toward an end. • Showing ( exemplar steering ). Instead of describing the target, you hand the model a batch of examples and ask for more like them. Sorted through the cheap label P P , that batch is a mix of bins — a recipe “70% beach scenes, 30% snow,” written μ P \mu_{P} . It is the mix, not the individual examples, that the move turns on, so from here we describe showing by its recipe μ P \mu_{P} over bins. In the picture: you choose which columns the batch comes from. You hand over examples, but what steers is the mix of bins they fall into — that is the one shift in vocabulary to keep. Telling works one column; showing weights different columns. They reach different parts of the picture. We make all of this precise next. Two budgets The total spread of L L — its variance across the data — splits cleanly into the two parts the picture shows, and each move draws on one: Figure 2: The variance budget: the total spread of L splits into the within-column part (the within-bin budget, telling) and the between-column part (the between-bin budget, showing). ( Schematic — illustrative numbers, not measured data; the measured crystal split, e.g. band gap E / ( E + T ) = 0.98 E/(E{+}T)=0.98 , is in Evidence §4.) • Telling draws on the spread within a column — the within-bin budget T T . • Showing draws on the spread between columns — the between-bin budget E E . They sum to the whole spread, exactly: Var 𝒥 ​ ( L ) = ∑ b w b ​ v b ⏟ T ​ (within) + ∑ b w b ​ ( g b − g ¯ ) 2 ⏟ E ​ (between) , g ¯ = ∑ b w b ​ g b . \mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{J}}(L)\;=\;\underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{b}w_{b}\,v_{b}}_{T\ \text{(within)}}\;+\;\underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{b}w_{b}\,(g_{b}-\bar{g})^{2}}_{E\ \text{(between)}},\qquad\bar{g}=\textstyle\sum_{b}w_{b}\,g_{b}. A budget is a variance — the room available, nothing more. It says how far a property could be moved, not what any particular move does with it. The two moves each draw on one budget. Telling reweights within a bin, so it draws on T T ; showing reweights across bins with the recipe μ P \mu_{P} , so it draws on E E . Either way, the move shifts the average L L of what you generate, and that shift is at most χ 2 ⋅ budget \sqrt{\chi^{2}\cdot\text{budget}} — where χ 2 \chi^{2} measures how hard the move pushes from the original mix. The budgets are fixed by the three numbers, before the model is built . So the deciding difference between the moves is not how hard you push but which budget each can touch at all — T T for telling, E E for showing. Telling cannot cross bins. We have written the goal as the batch’s average L L , but it can be any property of the batch — its spread, or whether it covers two kinds at once. Theory derives the bounds, unpacks χ 2 \chi^{2} , and shows which move each kind of goal needs. Data audit, model audit Everything so far has audited the training data 𝒥 \mathcal{J} — the budget is read off the data, before the model is even built. But what you ultimately care about is what the model produces: an audit of its own outputs, G \mathrm{G} . So why should the data audit tell you anything about the model’s? Because a generative model is trained to reproduce its data. For a property it reproduces well, the model’s outputs fall into the bins with the same shares, heights, and spreads as the data — the model audit matches the data audit — so the cheap data audit (no model, no sampling) stands in for it. The catch is that the model is not trained on your property L L . It is trained to reproduce the data as a whole — to predict the next token, to denoise toward real samples — and L L is just something you happen to care about. So the data audit stands in faithfully only when L L is something the model reproduces well. A crystal generator’s density — read straight off the shape it draws — comes out matching the data; its stability — an energy that a small error in the structure throws off — does not, and there the model audit drifts from the data’s. When you are not sure a property carries, don’t guess — check it: sample the model, audit those outputs, and compare them to the data’s bin by bin — the two numbers to read are the drift δ \delta (did the bin means move?) and the spread ratio ρ \rho (did the within-bin variety carry?). Application gives that check step by step, Evidence runs it across easy and hard properties in both domains, and Theory ’s Scope marks where the data audit holds and where it breaks. (A fine-tuned model reproduces a reshaped version of the data — Theory handles that too.) Every symbol above is also collected in a one-page table, grouped by kind, in the Appendix (§A0, Notation ) — for reference when a symbol turns up later without its introduction nearby. Where to go from here You now have the working picture — B B bins of L L , the two moves, the two budgets. The rest of the paper builds on it in order: • Theory derives where the two square-root bounds come from, shows how the choice of recipe μ P \mu_{P} scales showing’s reach (the χ 2 \chi^{2} factor), and states the falsifiable claims that follow — then closes with a short note on what this implies for familiar training phenomena (mode collapse, the alignment tax, and the like). (It also notes why variance is the right currency — a methodological choice: cruder measures like max-minus-min are noisy.) • Evidence tests those claims in two unrelated domains. • Application turns the result into a recipe: how to measure your own budget, tell whether telling already suffices, and pick the construction that closes the gap if it does not. A reader who wants the practice before the derivations can jump straight to Application and refer back. Theory — How far telling and showing reach Preliminaries set up the working picture and the two ways to steer. To recall: a generator G \mathrm{G} produces outputs D D ; a cheap key P = π ⁡ ( D ) P=\pi(D) sorts them into B B bins; the expensive target L = ψ ⁡ ( D ) L=\psi(D) fills each bin with a spread of values; and you steer L L two ways — telling stays inside one bin and nudges its outputs, while showing changes which bins the batch is drawn from. Preliminaries also named the two budgets — T T (within-bin) and E E (between-bin) — and their reaches. This section derives them. §1 shows how the total spread of L L splits into the two budgets. §2 derives how far each operation can move L L , how the recipe μ P \mu_{P} scales showing’s reach through a factor χ 2 \chi^{2} , and — given a goal — which operation it calls for and, when that is showing, the shape (curvature) of the recipe it needs. §3 states the falsifiable claims that follow, including how the data-side budget transfers to a real model. §4 then reads off what the budget implies for some familiar training phenomena, and §5 marks where the framework applies and where it stops. The detailed machinery, the case-by-case reach of each operation, and the full statement of the boundaries are in the Appendix . A practitioner can skip to Application . Recall the per-bin quantities: bin b b has share w b w_{b} , mean g b = 𝔼 𝒥 ​ [ L ∣ P b ] g_{b}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{J}}[L\mid P_{b}] , and within-bin variance v b = Var 𝒥 ​ [ L ∣ P b ] v_{b}=\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{J}}[L\mid P_{b}] . 1. The budget: one variance, split in two Take the property L L and ask where its variation across the data lives. Some sits within bins — outputs that share a key still differ in L L — and some sits between bins — different bins have different average L L . Those are the only two places it can live, and across the B B bins they add up exactly: Var 𝒥 ​ ( L ) ⏟ total = ∑ b w b ​ v b ⏟ T ​ (within-bin) + ∑ b w b ​ ( g b − g ¯ ) 2 ⏟ E ​ (between-bin) , g ¯ = ∑ b w b ​ g b . \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{J}}(L)}_{\text{total}}\;=\;\underbrace{\sum_{b}w_{b}\,v_{b}}_{T\ \text{(within-bin)}}\;+\;\underbrace{\sum_{b}w_{b}\,(g_{b}-\bar{g})^{2}}_{E\ \text{(between-bin)}},\qquad\bar{g}=\sum_{b}w_{b}\,g_{b}. T T is the within-bin spread averaged over bins — the room telling works in, since telling stays inside one bin. E E is the spread of the bin means — the room showing works in, since showing moves between bins. This identity is the law of total variance (Casella & Berger, 2002), exact for any ( π , L , 𝒥 ) (\pi,L,\mathcal{J}) — no overlap, no remainder. Its two terms are the room the two operations work in. The pieces here are elementary — the total-variance split and the Cauchy–Schwarz reweighting bound below are textbook; the contribution is not the mathematics but composing them into a cheap, pre-model, three-numbers-per-bin audit that forecasts the telling/showing crossover and, under a testable condition, carries to a trained model. Take two properties A A and B B , and mark each bin as a point on a plane — its mean of A A across, its mean of B B up. A recipe’s batch lands at the blend of those points, so its reachable averages fill the convex hull of the bins.
